This research investigates the quark-gluon plasma's composition, represented by flow fluctuations within heavy-ion collisions. Our study combines the recent CMS electron flow measurements at the LHC's 7 TeV proton-proton and lead-lead collision energies to create a unified description of the plasma's structural characteristics. By integrating the quark-gluon plasma's volume, elastic and inelastic scattering processes, and thermal correlations, we develop a multi-dimensional picture of the CMS experiment data. Furthermore, our analysis compares and contrasts this unified interpretation of the data against analogous results obtained using the LUCIFER hadron transport model, a sophisticated Monte Carlo simulation tool, to highlight any discrepancies and similarities with our quark-gluon plasma model. Our findings also shed light on the relative importance of initial conditions, transport coefficients, and elastic process re-scattering on the quark-gluon plasma's properties and flow fluctuations. Ultimately, this research enables a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between the quark-gluon plasma's composition, collision physics, and hadron transport theory. Our quark-gluon plasma parameter set, extracted directly from experimental data, may serve as a benchmark for future hadron transport model developments. Our analysis highlights key aspects of the quark-gluon plasma's composition that remain elusive to experimental measurements alone and require further theoretical and phenomenological study. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness using simulations and real-world data examples. Additionally, we apply TV-PARX to an analysis of the 2007 global financial crisis's impact on default rates, uncovering distinct time variations in default dynamics for pre-, during-, and post-crisis periods. This work contributes to the development of dynamic models capable of handling both extreme events and structural breaks, and highlights the potential benefits for companies seeking to better manage risk and credit default. Learning complex manipulation tasks requires a tremendous amount of data and time-consuming trial-and-error experimentation. To tackle this challenge, this paper presents Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a method for efficiently learning tasks from limited demonstrations. NDFs combine the benefits of neural descriptor learning and vector field optimization to discover underlying task representations. By positioning descriptors along the path connecting initial and goal states in a scene, NDFs determine the direction of optimization for each descriptor, effectively defining a potential function that steers the learning process. This function also serves as a task-relevant cost function, guiding the exploration for optimal actions. We demonstrate NDFs' capabilities on two demanding manipulation tasks: picking objects from cluttered shelves and assembling toy blocks according to precise instructions. In both scenarios, NDFs successfully learn from just five demonstrations each. Furthermore, NDFs excel when compared to alternative approaches and baselines, highlighting the versatility and efficiency of Neural Descriptor Fields in mastering challenging tasks with minimal guidance. The project code is available at https://github.com/PRPR-Lab/NDF.

Traditionally, AOD estimation relies on photometric zero-point calibration, but our research demonstrates the feasibility of an internal standard without absolute calibration. This approach leverages the unique combination of full-sky observations and considers the spatial distribution of light across the sky to derive aerosol depth information. In multilayer networks, nodes can hold different levels of importance across various connections. Researchers typically measure node importance using centrality metrics, but the impact of constraints across layers is often overlooked, leading to skewed results. To address this issue, we introduce the spread centrality measure, accounting for variations in importance between layers and within the network. Calculating this measure, we consider inter-layer constraints as referrals that direct attention to specific layers and nodes. This results in a system of equations reflecting the complex interplay of factors, and we provide a computational framework to solve it. Further, we discuss various optimization problems whose solutions correlate with spread centrality, and illustrate the concept using an example of a multilayer collaboration network. Empirical data shows that spread centrality accurately identifies key nodes that bridge gaps between layers, making it invaluable for network optimization and mapping. Moreover, due to its inter-layer nature, it offers a distinct view from traditional centrality measures. We have publicly available code to assist replication and new applications.

Experiments were conducted at the University of Michigan, with a high-speed camera capturing data at frame rates of up to 20,000 frames per second and pressures measured within the cavity through pressure sensors connected via a data acquisition system. Experiments were performed at various cavity pressures, with pressures inside the cavity ranging from 0 to 1.4 kPa, and a range of 0 to 6.3 m/s in jet velocities. High-speed imaging allowed for the frame-by-frame examination of seal surface dynamics and the detection of bubble formation within the cavity. Analysis revealed an increase in pressure within the cavity during the initial stages of the experiment, followed by a return to baseline levels. Additionally, higher cavity pressures were found to result in reduced pressures inside the cavity. Furthermore, the study observed that increased jet velocities led to a shift in the surface seal's state of oscillation, transitioning from a state of isolation to one of instability as the velocity exceeded 4.5 m/s. Strain on the flexible wall was found to increase with both cavity pressure and jet velocity, exhibiting a nonlinear response to changes in these variables. Lastly, the study noted that the pressure reduction inside the cavity acts as a key factor in surface seal dynamics, with the seal's state of oscillation being influenced by the interaction between the pressure reduction, the flexible wall's strain, and the rate of change in strain. Ultimately, the study demonstrated that the dynamics of the surface seal are affected by the interaction of multiple variables, with implications for understanding the behavior of pressurized flexible walls in a variety of scenarios. Given the limitations of the current study, further research is necessary to fully understand the effects of a range of fluid velocities on the surface seal of a cavity with a flexible wall. This paper introduces a concept called the generalized Witten effect to describe the behavior of an electrically charged field in gauge theory when its coupling is altered. This effect was initially observed by Edward Witten and has been updated to accommodate changes in the spectrum of charged states. By reinterpreting the generalized Witten effect through the lens of quantum gravity, we gather evidence that the entire spectrum of charged states is actually involved in the effect, leading to a revised understanding of its fundamental nature. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that the generalized Witten effect is, in fact, the manifestation of the quantum gravity theory's own charged states, which results from the interaction between the gauge theory and quantum gravity. By comparing this prediction with experimental data, we estimate the quantum gravity scale and present a theory that could potentially explain the observed phenomena, which was previously unexplained. This new theory, known as quantum gravity with a charged screening glue sector (QGCSS), offers predictions for future experiments and has distinct features that set it apart from other quantum gravity theories. We've developed a novel variational message passing method for approximating polymer distributions. This approximation represents a polymer as a tree structure, composed of its constituent monomers, which facilitates efficient inference. Our approach differs from existing variational methods by using a non-parametric representation that directly mirrors the polymer's physical structure. This allows us to bypass the traditional VVF-VAE framework, sidestepping the need to enforce a Gaussian distribution constraint. Our approach generates a variational distribution with a flexible form that aligns with the message passing dynamics, yielding precise reconstruction and excellent sampling performance. Moreover, our model succeeds in tackling a complex protein structure prediction task with remarkable results, surpassing the performance of leading baselines in multiple assessment metrics. All the code necessary for replicating our results is available at https://github.com/tingkelei/VAMP. This model's prowess in predicting protein structures has been demonstrated through submission to the CASP14 and CASP17 benchmarks, where it achieved rankings of 3.0 and 5.1, respectively, in the free model category. Additionally, our model has a linear scaling characteristic with respect to the size of the input data, making predictive predictions possible for large-scale molecular structures. This is due to its inherently efficient memory consumption, amounting to less than 10 GB when handling proteomes of the scale found in UniProt. This efficiency enables our model to tackle molecular biology problems involving 10,000s of residues, as showcased by a specific example where our model successfully predicted the structure of a 4700-residue long protein known as 'Supergiant Protein SG1' with remarkable accuracy. This prediction was achieved without the need for any initial structural data, relying instead on a proteome containing 1600 known protein structures and a set of general rules governing protein architecture, as detailed in the methods section below. This proteome comprises a dataset of 174,579 proteins with a total of 74 million residues, spanning 350,000 residues on average per protein, and is available at https://www.bigbigprotein.com/. This model's scalability is further highlighted by successful application to a task predicting 20% of a protein's residues with an accuracy of 70% or higher, which is equivalent to scanning the entire proteome for a given query in less than 10 seconds. In recent years, attention-based unet gained significant popularity among medical image segmentation techniques due to its superior performance. Our research builds upon DDUnet by introducing a novel variant, DDAUnet, tailored specifically to automate the segmentation of esophageal tumors from MRI scans. Our innovative contribution involves incorporating multi-scale, multi-level dense attention mechanisms within the unet framework to produce a concise and efficient model. DDAUnet is distinguished from its predecessors by utilizing spatial attention in both input and output feature maps to direct the information flow, resulting in a highly accurate and highly efficient model. Our experiments indicate that DDAUnet delivers a pAUC score of 0.959, an FDR of 0.155, a DSC of 0.623, a HA of 0.741, a SDR of 0.522, a MIoU of 0.624 in a dataset comprising 50 patients with abdominal respiratory motion, achieving a speed of 42ms per scan. Furthermore, DDAUnet demonstrates comparable performance to state-of-the-art models on publicly available medical datasets, including Multi-Organ PASCAL and LIT20x20. Our proprietary code is available online for public access.

In highly multilingual societies, NLP research can make a big difference, and we should conduct tests to evaluate our achievements. Developers often focus solely on evaluating models on tasks in their native language, ignoring how well they perform on foreign languages. To address this limitation, we created a comprehensive dataset consisting of 17 diverse languages, with both high and low resource texts for testing. We pre-trained a massive multilingual model on a vast dataset of 60 languages but tested it on our smaller dataset of 17 languages. Our results show that the model excels on languages with abundant texts but struggles with languages that have limited texts. To improve the model's performance, we developed three techniques: selecting the most linguistically similar languages, reducing noise in cross-language learning, and fine-tuning the model on our smaller dataset. By applying these techniques, we significantly enhanced the model's performance on all languages. To validate our findings, we conducted additional tests and compared our results to those from existing multilingual models. We also applied the model to two significant tasks: translating multiple sentences and summarizing text. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable data for further research in multilingual learning. This study uses Google's mobile user data to analyze the geographic patterns of online information dissemination within the US. A novel method was developed to assess the geographical clustering of search result sharing among nearby locations. The data reveals that search result sharing is significantly higher near urban centers and decreases with distance from these areas. Furthermore, a negative correlation was found between local search result sharing and population segregation in each region. Additionally, the study found that search result sharing is not solely explained by factors such as population density, internet access, or socioeconomic status. Ultimately, the research suggests that The Big Sort may exacerbate the spread of online misinformation among socially isolated individuals. A novel gradient flow formalism for quantum field theory, inspired by the Euler-Arnold equations, is proposed to interpret the Wilson-Polyakov line as a collective coordinate in quantum chromodynamics. This interpretation leads to the Euler-Arnold equations serving as gradient flow constraints, and enabling the derivation of a modified Wilson-Polyakov line operator. This operator, defined in terms of the trace of a heat evolved Polyakov loop, results in the Euler-Arnold equations acting as its definition, and it exhibits a shifted deconfinement transition in Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, this new construction implies an intuitive explanation for the Euler-Arnold equations in terms of local gauge ensemble averages. In addition, a modified extensive gauge invariant version of the Wilson-Polyakov line operator is introduced, and its properties in Monte Carlo simulations are contrasted with the original operator. This new approach is compatible with the conventional definition of the Wilson-Polyakov line operator in the limit of zero time interval, and provides an explicit distinction between the confinement transition and the deconfinement transition. This framework also offers an interpretation for the recently discovered effects of the quantum chromodynamics vacuum, such as the mass scale generation and the theta vacuum dynamics, in terms of the dynamics of gauge field configurations in gauge ensemble, defined by the Euler-Arnold equations. This new construction's validity is demonstrated in lattice quantum chromodynamics simulations with finite temperature and zero chemical potential. This new approach's scope is not limited to quantum chromodynamics, as the Euler-Arnold equations represent a general mathematical framework, applicable to any gauge theory. Conversational system testing frameworks face several challenges in scaling automated tests due to the exponential growth of possible user inputs and system responses. This growth limits the practical size of test suites constructed through traditional automated testing methods. In response to this challenge, researchers have been exploring machine learning models to generate effective tests for conversational systems at a larger scale. Although promising, the current state of such models is not well understood, as research data is scarce and difficult to obtain. To address these challenges, a new dataset called TestGenData was created, comprising 15,000 distinct data points for training a model that can generate conversational system test inputs. This model exhibits a 6.7% increase in accuracy when tested on its own, and a 10.6% improvement when evaluated using a theoretical test suite. Furthermore, the associated code enables easy replication of the approach using the developed models. Our primary goal is to enhance the recommendation system's ability to learn user preferences by capturing the diverse aspects present in item descriptions. The key challenge we face is preventing the representation of user preferences from being dominated by the abundant surface information found in these descriptions. To address this challenge, we develop the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, a novel and straightforward component that accurately identifies relevant aspects and associated preferences from the input item descriptions. By leveraging the GAPE module in a neural cooperative learning framework, we are able to effectively learn the representation of user preferences. Our proposed approach surpasses multiple baseline models, achieving the best recommendation performance on public datasets. Moreover, the comparative analysis of different component modifications provides valuable insights into optimizing user preference learning. In addition to the improvements it offers, GAPE also enhances the understanding of user preference learning by highlighting the differences between relevant and irrelevant aspects as well as the surface information that aspects are associated with. In addition to its primary application in recommendation systems, GAPE has the potential to be beneficial for other diverse tasks that involve aspect-level representation and learning from text data. In order to facilitate further research, we have made the code and models publicly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/Chang32089930/GAPE. In summary, our main contributions are as follows. First, we have proposed a novel and straightforward component known as the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module that is capable of accurately identifying relevant aspects and associated preferences from the input item descriptions. In addition, we have developed a neural cooperative learning framework that leverages the GAPE component to effectively learn the representation of user preferences. Furthermore, we have comparative analysis of different component modifications, which provides valuable insights into optimizing user preference learning as well as highlighting the differences between relevant and irrelevant aspects along with the surface information that aspects are associated with. Cutting plane methods are a primary technique for solving LP relaxations, which are derived from the original problem and represent its extended form. However, the dimensionality and difficulty of these natural formulations can vary significantly for different problems. To better understand the underlying structure of these formulations, researchers have been examining the most basic form - formulations using exotic cones - which are directly linked to the concept of extended formulations. To this end, a new framework has been established that compares the natural formulations using exotic cones to their equivalent forms using extended formulations. This comparison is quantified through the use of specific dimensions, including the number of variables and constraints in both formulations. A particular case study is then presented, showcasing the applicability of this framework, as it reduces the well-known cut-cone formulation from a dimension of 2 to 1. Additionally, a general approach is outlined for determining the optimal form of any natural formulation using an exotic cone, by leveraging the principles of strong LP relaxations and the theory of extended formulations. Furthermore, the limitations of this research also prompt a broader discussion on the distinct types of complexity exhibited by natural and extended formulations. It is demonstrated that the $n$-dimensional cube can be represented using a natural formulation with an exotic cone of the rank $2^n$, as well as the 0-1 knapsack constraint, which both display uniquely distinct forms of complexity. It is shown that the rank of both these exotic cones corresponds to the largest possible rank among all extended formulations equivalent to them, utilizing the established framework. It is also proven that the rank of an extended formulation is directly linked to its size, as well as the size of its equivalent strong LP relaxation. It is further shown that the rank of an exotic cone is the minimum possible size among all natural formulations equivalent to it. It is also demonstrated that the use of the projective reduction does not alter the dimensionality of these exotic cones, which is in turn linked to the deepest level of nesting in their defining equations. It is also shown that the deepest level of nesting is directly linked to the height of the corresponding LP relaxation, which in turn is indicative of the difficulty of the natural formulation. It is also demonstrated that the height of the LP relaxation is the minimum possible size among all natural formulations equivalent to a given exotic cone. It is also shown that the number of variables in an exotic cone is the maximum possible size among all extended formulations equivalent to it. The rapid advancement of deep learning techniques has led to a surge in utility AI, where it's essential to ensure that models behave fairly and effectively, even when exposed to substantial amounts of new, unseen data. We examine the robustness of a state-of-the-art MRI reconstruction model when it's trained on substantial amounts of diverse medical data. Our research used a diverse dataset comprising 100,000 MRI scans from 50 different datasets, consisting of both normal and pathological images. The model achieved remarkable reconstruction performance, obtaining a mean absolute error of 6.2 and a structural similarity index of 88.3 on unseen data. Furthermore, our study revealed that the model's performance declined only marginally when exposed to new, unseen MRI data, indicating a high degree of robustness. We also compared the model's performance to a naive approach involving random sampling from the training set. This comparison revealed that the model's performance plateaus when the sample size exceeds 10,000, suggesting that it can effectively utilize sparse representations to focus on key features even when exposed to large amounts of new data. The model's robustness was further demonstrated by minimal performance degradation when reconstructing degraded or artificially manipulated MRI images. This model has been integrated into an interactive tool that enables healthcare professionals to explore MRI reconstruction with different protocols and protocols combinations at the following address: https://healthcare.deepmind.com/mri-explorer. This research was conducted in collaboration with the University College London and the University of Edinburgh. This paper introduces a framework for network-based multi-agent optimization issues, incorporating constraints and objective functions that link agents through a communication network. A novel decomposition approach is then developed to solve general problems within this framework, involving a centralized component that manages the network and related variables, and a decentralized component that handles individual agent optimizations. A key aspect of this decomposition is the incorporation of an edge-variable expansion technique to facilitate further decomposition of connected components of the network. In addition to its general applicability, this framework and decomposition method are specifically demonstrated to solve a particular multi-agent issue known as the minimum connection cost cut problem. Numerical examples are used to compare the performance of this decomposition against existing methods for two particular applications: the minimum connection cost flow problem and the stochastic knapsack problem. Numerous test cases are also used to evaluate the efficacy of this decomposition approach through various scalability tests. However, the charmed baryon family, which includes producers like Lambda_c and Sigma_c, require further study. The spatial diffusion of optical spectra can be utilized to investigate defects in solid materials, especially for quantum technology applications. Previously, research has primarily analyzed individual defects, but a study for T centre ensembles in diamond reveals a unique pattern of spectral shifting tied to their spatial distribution. By identifying the underlying diffusion processes, researchers aim to uncover the fundamental physics driving these phenomena and explore their potential utility in quantum technology development. A novel approach is presented that combines spatial and spectral analysis to reveal the diffusion patterns of T centre ensembles and related features. The study further reveals that the diffusion of these patterns is influenced by both the high temperature phonon absorption background and the presence of neighbouring defects. By removing these distortions, the original diffusion patterns can be reconstituted, providing valuable insights into the distribution of defects and potentially informing strategies for their controlled placement. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the characteristic diffusion of optical spectra can serve as a distinctive identity for T centre ensembles, facilitating efficient sorting and filtering based on their spatial distribution. Furthermore, the findings offer a foundation for exploring quantum solid-state systems with precisely positioned defects, presenting a promising avenue for quantum technology advancement. The developed approach is applicable to T centre ensembles in both diamond with nitrogen vacancies and diamond with boron substitutions, and the methodological framework is adaptable for extension to other quantum systems with precisely positioned defects. Additionally, the study highlights the efficacy of a novel sorting algorithm that efficiently identifies and separates ensemble diffusion patterns based on predefined criteria, demonstrating the utility of this approach for controlled defect placement and related quantum technology development. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of spatial diffusion to serve as a solid-state classical precursor for quantum properties, with the developed approach showcasing a future direction for quantum technology that relies on the precise positioning of defects within materials. The characteristic diffusion patterns of T centre ensembles can persist up to 550 K, and the associated phonon absorption background can be accurately removed to reconstitute the original diffusion patterns. The development of a novel algorithm for sorting ensemble diffusion patterns based on their spatial distribution is also presented, in addition to a discussion on the future directions for quantum systems with precisely positioned defects, such as N<sub>5</sub> centres in diamond and WB pairs in diamond. The effectiveness of the introduced approach is demonstrated in both type Ia and IIa diamond, as well as in diamonds with varying boron concentrations. Deep neural network-based object detectors have varying performances in different scenarios and depend heavily on the underlying data they are trained on. Because of the numerous object detection algorithms available, selecting the most suitable one for a given context can be very challenging. To address this issue, a framework called Context-Agnostic Object Detector (CAD) was developed to facilitate the inference process across different contexts by employing a small set of features as input. CAD was designed to be context-agnostic on its own, but it can be trained to be context-specific to improve its performance. By combining CAD with a context-aware selector, it is capable of adapting to new contexts with minimal training data. Experimental evaluations conducted on four datasets revealed CAD's effectiveness in versatile object detection tasks. Additionally, a novel evaluation metric called Average Selective Context Adaptation (ASCA) was introduced to assess a detector's ability to adapt to new contexts. ASCA was demonstrated to correlate positively with the increase in context-aware performance. Moreover, a comparative analysis was performed between fine-tuning the entire network and adapting it to a specific context, and the results showed that context-adaptable detectors are more efficient in terms of data required for adaptation. In recent years, significant progress has been made in designing algorithms for optimal kidney matching under waiting time constraints, thanks in part to incompatibility costs being treated as a state variable in Markov Decision Processes. However, considering incompatibility costs in this manner assumes they are one-dimensional, which is not the case in reality, as they are typically multi-dimensional. Our research addresses this limitation by developing an explicit framework for analyzing the problem and showing that under certain conditions, it is equivalent to a multi-dimensional Markov Decision Process with multiple objectives. Furthermore, we offer a distinct single-dimensional perspective by formulating the problem as a sequence of separate Markov Decision Processes, which we term the `incompatibility ladders'. In wideband waveforming, allocating subbands based on channel state information can yield significant performance benefits. This study investigates optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput waveforming strategies, taking into account the costs of data refarming. A key finding shows that the optimal fair-throughput solution can be obtained using a rounding method, resulting in a linear program with a feasible region defined by the rounded Matroid Polytope. Furthermore, the study establishes that the rounded Matroid Polytope is equivalently represented by the cut-linear system of the Interlacing Theorem from the theory of special matrices. Additionally, the study reveals that the optimal sum-throughput solution can be determined using an integer linear program with a specific structure, allowing for the extraction of lower and upper bounds using linear programming relaxation. Moreover, the study provides an algorithm for solving an instance of the problem by combining the integer linear program with variable elimination, leading to a product-of-linear-programmes-type relaxation. The proposed algorithm achieves a degree of success in solving instances of the problem, particularly in the regime where the number of subbands exceeds the number of users. The study also includes numerical results illustrating the performance benefits of fair and sum-throughput waveforming strategies in various network settings. This research proposes a novel complex-valued physics-informed neural network (PINN) for analyzing the Rayleigh-Benard instability in convective fluids. We recognize that traditional PDE solvers face significant difficulties when dealing with nonlinear neural networks, and this method addresses those challenges by employing a complex-valued architecture. Two key innovations are introduced: a way to reduce the number of PDE constraints and an optimization technique based on the complex-valued Adam optimizer. Our solution employs a neural network with a complex-valued structure to efficiently solve a set of PDE constraints and the associated Neumann boundary conditions for the complex-valued function. This results in two separate sets of real-valued PDEs and Neumann conditions for the network's real and imaginary components. We further introduce a method to minimize the PDE residual for both the real and imaginary components of the network, utilizing the Adam optimizer in a complex-valued format. This technique significantly improves the convergence of the optimization process. Our solution was tested on multiple problem domains, ranging from a simple one-dimensional PDE to complex PDE networks, and has been applied to the study of convective fluid instability. We're examining the dynamic changes in a basic model of network epidemics, where the community in question is not static. We have a model where the network adapts by randomly disconnecting a small number of unimportant connections and replacing them with new ones to both existing partners and a large pool of potential new ones. As this dynamic process continues, we observe a surprising phenomenon - a significant reduction in the number of people infected during an epidemic. To better understand this observed decrease, we developed a simple static model that includes the same core features as the dynamic network, but in a non-changing format. This allowed us to gain insight into the dynamics of the dynamic model and network epidemics in general. Some of the notable findings include the creation of power-law distributions of connection durations and the formation of assortative communities based on connection properties. We also discovered that these features significantly contribute to a decrease in the number of people infected during an epidemic. Additionally, we found that the dynamic network exhibits a high level of resilience, both in its ability to withstand attacks and recover from them. We believe that these findings provide a valuable understanding of network epidemics in complex dynamic communities and can serve as a foundation for further research and more complex models. To facilitate this, we have made the code for our model publicly available. We also introduced two new metrics, the Assortative Mixing Ratio and the Community Assortativity, that we feel are valuable tools for evaluating the properties of dynamic networks and mixed-strategy interactions. We encourage their use and feedback on them to help improve them. We hope that our research will contribute to a greater understanding of dynamic networks and the epidemics that spread through them, as well as the other complex phenomena that occur within them. We also want to emphasize the potential applications of our findings in areas such as public health policy and internet management. We feel that our simple dynamic model captures the core features of a wide range of more complex networks and scenarios, but we acknowledge that it has its limitations and we encourage the testing of our results and the exploration of new ideas within the community of network researchers. We would like to express our gratitude to the researchers whose work has contributed to ours, as well as the Australian Research Council for the funding that we received. We also thank the researchers at the University of Melbourne, the University of Sydney, the University of Queensland, the University of Technology in Sydney, the University of Wollongong, the University of Newcastle, the University of Adelaide, the University of Tasmania, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Organisation, the Melbourne Institute

This paper presents a new approach to determining parton distribution functions (PDFs) by using evolutionary equations to connect different energy scales, as proven in previous work. We have now applied this concept to a modified version of the DGLAP evolution equation and incorporated lattice QCD data from Monte Carlo simulations from the Chrono-Hermite interpolation method. By taking this lattice QCD data at a fixed, high energy scale, we have fitted for the PDFs and successfully tested the fit's validity by verifying that the fitted PDFs accurately reconstruct the original lattice data when evolved to the same energy scale. Furthermore, we have successfully validated our PDF fit at a lower energy scale, which is more relevant for quarkonium studies, by employing the improved kernel perturbative approach. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of using lattice QCD data to determine PDFs at moderate energy scales and lay the groundwork for utilizing this approach in conjunction with experimental data from quarkonium production studies. The PDF fit we have developed has the added benefit of eliminating the need to adjust the renormal group evolution evolution constant, as evidenced by the fit's ability to reproduce the correct value for this constant as part of the PDF fit. The PDF fit we have created also exhibits an exceptionally high level of stability across a wide range of lattice QCD simulation configurations. The PDFs we have determined through this approach exhibit a comparable level of accuracy to those produced using contemporary PDF fitting methods, which are based on deep learning models, as demonstrated by a comparison of predicted hadron fragmentation functions. The methodology we have developed is highly versatile and can be applied to the determination of PDFs for quarks and gluons within hadrons of various types, as well as hadron distribution functions within quarkonia and other composite systems. The chronology-independent nature of the Chrono-Hermite method ensures that the PDFs we have determined are insensitive to the simulation configuration's chronological characteristics. The set of lattice QCD data we have employed has been previously validated through tests of translational symmetry, chronology independence, and correct asymptotic behavior in the ultraviolet regime. The energy scale at which we have fitted the PDFs is within the range of scales for which the DGLAP evolution equation remains applicable, according to the value of the strong coupling constant calculated using the renormalization group. The variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework is introduced, which reformulates the policy gradient estimation problem to provide a data-efficient solution when collecting samples is costly. The framework yields a general theorem on policy gradient estimation with the variance reduced method, leveraging experience data. A specific implementation of the VRER framework is then presented for continuous action spaces, resulting in the variance reduced policy gradient estimator. This new estimator is compared to existing methods and demonstrated to offer improved data efficiency in policy gradient estimation. Experimental evaluations across multiple scenarios highlight the effectiveness of the variance reduced policy gradient estimator. The approach is further applied to the experience replay based actor-learning algorithm, leading to a centralized actor-learning algorithm. The experience data required for policy gradient estimation can take various forms, but the common aspect is that collecting new samples is costly, making the application of the VRER framework valuable across different domains. In dialog generation tasks, understanding the other party's mental state, or theory of mind, is crucial for generating appropriate responses. While this capability improves with training on vast amounts of text, the underlying basis remains unexplored. Our research delves into the theory of mind aspect of dialog generation through a novel, controlled setup where we craft questions to assess the generated text's alignment with the listener's mental state. To tackle this challenge, we develop a specialized neural dialog generation model and integrate a massive pre-trained language model to fine-tune the dialog generation task. Our results show that the models struggle to grasp the underlying theory of mind in the questions, highlighting a significant gap in their capabilities. To bridge this gap, we train the models on ethnotheory of mind statements, drawn from a custom-made dataset, and test their capacity on the original set of questions. Our findings indicate that the models succeed in solving the majority of questions about the speaker's mental state but consistently fail to solve those concerning the listener's mental state. In both cases, the model's performance improves when confronted with statements about the corresponding theory of mind. Our research sheds light on the limited theory of mind of neural dialog generation models and highlights the potential of ethnotheory of mind as a training data source to enhance their capabilities. To facilitate replication and advancement, we open-source our code and make ethnotheory of mind data generation methods available on GitHub. To gain a deeper understanding of how genetic sequences influence phenotypic variations, we examined the interplay between protein sequences and phenotype-associated SNPs within different biological traits. Using high-quality human protein data and a large-scale genetic study, we analyzed the hierarchical relationships among 5,501 associated SNPs, 17,925 protein-coding variants, and 23,500 human protein sequences. Our research uncovered a complex, three-dimensional structure representing the interconnections among these biological elements. By exploring this structure, we identified distinct clusters of associated SNPs, protein-coding variants, and nearby amino acid residues that share similar trait-related patterns. These clusters, which exhibit varying degrees of similarity to each other, are scattered across the three-dimensional structure. Our findings reveal that the influence of protein sequences on associated SNPs is neither fixed nor linear, and that the effects are instead multi-dimensional and cluster-dependent. Ultimately, our three-dimensional framework provides a nuanced explanation for the varied effects of SNPs on different traits, and highlights the central role that protein sequences play in mediating the relationships between genetic variants, biological traits, and environmental factors. Our research also introduces a novel approach for accurately predicting the traits associated with new SNPs, and showcases the utility of this method through a study of drug side effects. Researchers anticipate an increase in strange quark production, particularly strangeness enhancement, characterized by an increase in strange hadron production in heavy-ion collisions compared to the production in proton-proton collisions. A proposed study aims to conduct a detailed analysis of strange hadron production in proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions at the LHC with the ALICE detector. The methods also consider distinguishing hadronic decay modes from direct photon decay modes and suppressing background from light-flavor hadrons. A proposed upgrade to the ALICE detector, the Scalable Slice Extractor, is necessary to efficiently detect these particles. The design of the new detector and the proposed study are feasible with the current ALICE infrastructure. A detailed cost estimate for the upgrade is also provided. The Galactic bulac population of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LM X-rays) and millisecond radio pulsars (msPulsars) share a common precursor context. Both populations are thought to originate from the same evolution path, inspired by observations of the Large Magellanic Cloud and globular clusters. By examining the LM X-ray population in the Galaxy's center, this research discovered a significant discrepancy in the MSRP to LM X-ray ratio, estimated to be less than expected by a factor of fifteen. Furthermore, the LM X-ray population in the Galaxy's center appears to be composed of two subpopulations with distinct orbital periods, and both display reduced MSRP to LM X-ray ratios. Consequently, the hypothesis that all LM X-rays transform into msPulsars is challenged, and it is proposed that some LM X-rays may terminate their evolution within a compact disk, instead of shedding it and becoming a pulsar visible in radio. This study also presents a revised upper limit for the total LM X-ray population in the Galaxy's center, estimated as twenty-five. Additionally, the research updates the current LM X-ray population in the Galaxy's center to include X-ray sources from the TAO and SXT databases, incorporating orbital periods for twenty-nine sources. Moreover, a minimum mass loss rate required for LM X-ray sources to become msPulsars is proposed, and it is suggested that the necessary mass loss for this transition may result in some LM X-rays expending their angular momentum without becoming pulsars visible in radio. This study also examines the possible causes of msPulsars with companions more massive than the Chandrasekhar limit, and it is proposed that the necessary mass transfer to become an msPulsar may occur in some cases without fully reconciling the issue. Finally, an algorithm is presented for generating simulated populations of LM X-ray sources and msPulsars based on observable characteristics, and it is applicable to any Galactic environment surveyed. This research primarily focuses on the Galactic bulac, but the developed algorithm is suitable for application to any cluster or galaxy surveyed. This study also includes an examination of the necessary observations to determine the population of LM X-ray sources with short orbital periods in the Galaxy's center. Such a survey would require the use of an X-ray telescope with a large effective collection area and a optical/infrared survey of the Galactic center habitant. It is proposed that a future mission with both an X-ray and an optical/infrared component would be highly beneficial in accurately defining the population of LM X-ray

Quantum control over chemical reaction barriers is crucial for the development of efficient and selective chemical reactions. By leveraging the influence of vibrational modes on potential energy surfaces, it's possible to achieve this control. In this research, we investigate the coupling of a reaction barrier to quantum states of a specific vibrational mode, which we call the "doorway state". By targeting this state, we can manage the reaction barrier's quantum characteristics and thus the reaction rate. A novel approach to quantum control is introduced, based on the reaction barrier's quantum properties and the temporary attachment of a photon to the doorway state. This method allows for the broadening of the doorway state, the coupling to other quantum states, and the optimization of reaction rate spectra. By employing a genetic algorithm, we can successfully manage the reaction barrier's quantum characteristics, leading to a significant increase in the reaction rate at 532 nm and a decrease in the width of the reaction rate spectrum. Additionally, this approach is effective for various initial conditions of the reaction barrier and vibrational modes. In this research, we focus on a specific chemical reaction, but the introduced method is applicable to any reaction barrier influenced by a doorway state.

Human dialogue involves more than just exchanging information; it also requires exploring various dialogue topics and navigating through complex, nuanced social situations. Current dialogue models generate responses that prioritize coherence over semantic variety, often leading to limited and inaccurate inferences. To overcome this limitation, our research introduces a novel generative model called Diversity Explorer, comprising two primary components that tackle distinct challenges. Firstly, to circumvent the limitations of maximally likely generation, Diversity Explorer employs a sampling-based approach that leverages the strengths of both the conditional language model and the starter word's context. Secondly, to tackle the paradox of simultaneously increasing both coherence and diversity, the model employs a variety of starting words to generate a pool of responses, from which the most coherent ones are selected. Experimentation across multiple evaluation metrics reveals substantial improvements in generating diverse and coherent dialogue responses. Our pre-trained Diversity Explorer model is available for download at https://github.com/ghru/diversity-explorer. When applied to open-ended dialogue generation, it achieves a semantic scope increase of 37.8% and a coherence score boost of 13.1% when compared to a standard maximum likelihood generation approach. Furthermore, when employed for guided dialogue generation, it demonstrates the capability to accurately adhere to intricate guidance specifications comprising multiple constraints. Our research demonstrates substantial gains in generating diverse and coherent dialogue responses, across various evaluation metrics, and our model is ready for use at https://github.com/ghru/diversity-explorer. Our evaluation code can be found at https://github.com/ghru/divex-eval. Our approach is versatile and may be applied to other text generation tasks that necessitate the exploration of intricate semantic spaces. Hydrogen burning in low-mass stars is influenced by rotational energy and angular momentum. To better understand this process, we examine the critical parameters for hydrogen burning in stars with masses less than the solar mass. We analyze the interactions between angular momentum, rotation, hydrogen burning, and mass loss near the hydrogen-burning threshold. For envelope-hydrogen masses between 0.018 and 0.080 solar masses and surface temperatures between 3.5 kK and 4.4 kK, we identify the hydrogen-burning branch in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. By comparing observations of substellar objects like brown dwarfs, we find that the hydrogen-burning branch is affected by factors like metallicity, mass loss, and rotation. For example, we find that the 2.5 micron magnetic field can influence the hydrogen-burning branch, causing it to branch in a different direction. Additionally, we find that the angular momentum threshold, above which strong differential rotation occurs, significantly impacts the critical curves for hydrogen burning. For example, above 10^10 erg cm-2 s-2, the curvature becomes distorted, and above 1.75 x 10^10 erg cm-2 s-2, it becomes ring-shaped. Moreover, we find that the curvature can be influenced by the angular momentum threshold, mass loss, and envelope-hydrogen mass, and that it can be used to infer the mass loss and angular momentum of low-mass stars. We also examine the hydrogen-burning branch in the mass-temperature diagram for different angular momentum thresholds and mass loss rates. Furthermore, we compare our results with observations of brown dwarfs like LHS 625 and WPM AQL 1, which exhibit retretrograde rotation and fast rotation, respectively. Finally, we discuss the limitations of our study, including the need to consider additional factors like stellar oscillations, magnetic fields, and convection, which can influence the hydrogen-burning branch in low-mass stars. We also highlight potential future research directions, including the investigation of hydrogen-burning branches in different chemical compositions and the development of observational methods to measure mass loss and angular momentum in low-mass stars. Additionally, we outline possible future targets for studying hydrogen-burning branches in low-mass stars, including ultracool dwarfs, brown dwarfs with magnetic fields, and low-mass stars with retired planetary companions. We also discuss the potential for direct detection of hydrogen-burning branches in low-mass stars through spectroscopy and direct imaging

This method involves training neural network density models using fast sampling techniques and advanced optimization methods. Multiple tests demonstrate significant improvements in achieving stable fixed points when employing neural networks, compared to traditional GenEvT methods. Furthermore, this framework leads to a significant reduction in the variance of sampling data, allowing for Hadron Decays analyses with multiple decay channels. A key aspect explored in this research involves optimizing neural network density models for the correct slope parameter in thermal lattice QCD. This enables accurate estimation of hadron decay widths within the QCD phase diagram, extending beyond the transition region. Quantifying ultra-long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) in the high-relativity and non-relativity regimes remains a challenge. Afterglows in these regimes are difficult to model as they are influenced by various factors such as jet properties, the properties of the progenitor, and the energy of the expelling winds. A new model aims to address this challenge by combining various observations and theoretical constraints into a single equation. This model eliminates the need for separate models for ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic afterglows by incorporating a variable relativistic factor. By comparing the model with multiple GRB observations, the variable relativistic factor was found to range from 0.08 to 0.5 and was found to be directly correlated with the GRB's energy and duration. Furthermore, the model also explains the extended durations of GRBs born from neutron star mergers or supernoviae, and suggests that the most enduring GRBs are likely produced by massive jets breaking through massive progenitor winds. Additionally, the model predicts the range of wavelengths that GRB electromagnetic emissions will shift to in the near future. Based on the model, future observations with the Square Kilometre Array and the James Webb Space Telescope will likely detect the emissions from GRBs with durations of up to 100 seconds. Furthermore, the model anticipates that future observations will reveal a significant increase in GRB detections in the near-infrared and optical spectra, particularly in the GRBs born from neutron star mergers or supernoviae. Additionally, the model suggests that future observations will reveal a significant shift in the wavelengths of GRB electromagnetic emissions, particularly in the optical and near-infrared spectra, and will likely extend the duration of which we can study GRBs by up to a factor of ten. The model also enables the prediction of the energy and peak magnitude of GRB afterglows in the optical and near-infrared spectra with a margin of error of 0.5. The new model has been validated by comparing its predictions with multiple GRB observations and has significant implications for future GRB observations and the study of neutron star mergers and supernoviae. A bipartite graph can be rendered planar if non-split vertices are positioned on one side and edge junctions are on the other. If vertex splitting is an option, determining the minimum number of required split vertices to draw the graph planarly becomes an interesting problem. Resolving this dilemma was first proposed by Mercuri in 1999. Our study aims to automate this process for any bipartite graph by utilizing a two-step process. Firstly, the graph is converted into its maximum planar subgraph form, leaving only the necessary edge crossings. Then, the remaining edge crossings are navigated to identify the necessary split vertices. The time complexity of this approach is evaluated as O(n^2), where n represents the number of vertices within the graph. A comparative analysis is also conducted to assess the efficacy of this method in comparison to alternative existing solutions. Our approach has the added benefit of producing a drawing with the minimum number of edge crossings, and in the process, it can also determine the planar embeddability of a graph and identify the subgraphs that are congruent to Disjoint Crossings with Two Paths, all for the same time complexity of O(n^2). This approach was initially presented at the graph drawing and visualization conference in 2013. In addition to this, a new measure of graph planarity named Disjoint Crossings Number is introduced, which serves as an extension of the genus parameter. This new measure is then utilized to define a set of projections that are equivalent to DC2P, and in doing so, a (delta+1) approximation algorithm is achieved for this problem, with a time complexity of O(n^2). This was initially presented at the international colloquium on automata, languages and programming in 2011. A further contribution is the creation of a language that can be used to describe the projections that are equivalent to DC2P, for which a (delta+1) approximation algorithm is also defined, with a time complexity of O(n^2). This was initially presented at the international colloquium on automata, languages and programming in 2011. A further contribution is the creation of a language that can be used to describe the projections that are equivalent to DC2P, for which a learner is also defined, with a time complexity of O(n^2). This research investigates the performance enhancement of a bipedal robot in a dynamic environment through closed-loop feedback control. A key aspect of bipedal robots is their ability to adapt to changing situations, which can be facilitated by feedback control, allowing them to recover from disturbances and walk on varying terrain, among other benefits. However, implementing closed-loop control during a gait cycle is complex due to the varying contact conditions and foot placement, making it crucial to prioritize the feedback control for the most critical phases of the gait cycle. A central pattern generator (CPG) based control framework is employed to control the hip joints of the robot, while a simple foot placement strategy is used for the ankle joints. Additionally, a feedback control system is applied to the ankle joints during the single support phase to ensure stable foot placement. This approach enables the robot to walk on unstable platforms, adjust its gait to avoid obstacles, and modulate foot placement to improve stability. Moreover, the controller helps the robot to adjust its gait to prevent the heel from lifting off the ground, thus enhancing overall stability. A simulation-based evaluation of the controller was conducted prior to experimenting with a physical bipedal robot. The results show significant improvements in the robot's ability to walk on a balance board, decrease foot lift, and increase step length, which can be beneficial for various applications including agriculture, search and rescue, and long-distance walking. The code for this research is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/roboticauy/BipedalRobotFeedbackControl. The physical experiment was carried out at the Universidad del Valle, Cali, Colombia. The simulation environment was created using SimulationX 3.6 and the controller was programmed using MATLAB R2019b. The robot was programmed using the Robot Operating System (ROS) with the Ubuntu 18.04 operating system. The results of the experiment were analyzed using the statistical software R version 4.0.3. The design of the robot and the feedback controller was inspired by the research conducted by McGeer and colleagues, which was published in the paper "Impedance control of the CMIP biped" in the year 2011. The research presented in this paper was conducted at the Universidad de San Francisco de Quito, Ecuador, in the year 2020. The duration of the research project was six months. This conclusion can be contrasted with the fact that the field of formal Laurent series in one variable does not have a decidable first-order theory within its standard topology, as proven by Denef and Lipshitz in 1979. This achievement is reached through the development of several key techniques, including an innovative application of an infinite sequence of expanding polynomials to tackle quantifier inequalities and an infinite sequence of expanding power series to address unquantified inequalities. Moreover, this result extends the earlier result by Denef and Lipshitz from the finite characteristic case to the characteristic zero case, achieved via the application of p-adic analysis to extend results from the p-adic integers to the rational numbers. This enables us to combine these two results, merging their respective proofs into a single, unified approach. This work also includes an examination of the differences in approach and the distinct challenges posed by the characteristic zero case. Previous research revealed the effectiveness of Flush+Reload attacks, which leverage memory deallocation and reallocation functions to uncover sensitive information, including encryption keys and authentication tokens. However, such attacks are notoriously time-consuming and require a significant number of memory allocations and deallocations to overcome statistical fluctuations in memory state. A recent finding highlighted the potential for HyperDegrade, a technique that exploits page mapping events for similar attacks, and demonstrated the viability of targeting specific page mappings for token disclosure in XOR-Flash+Reload attacks. Building upon this discovery, our research introduces a novel approach, called HyperFlush+Reload, which successfully executes attacks on real-time systems using just one memory allocation and deallocation operation per target token. By tailoring attacks to specific page mappings and combining them with Flush+Reload techniques, HyperDegrade-enabled attackers can release memory pages that contain necessary page mappings, allowing for token retrieval in as little as 10 microseconds. Moreover, our experimentation on various real-time systems reveals the feasibility of carrying out attacks on multiple tokens within the same process, as well as the exploitation of tokens stored in kernel memory spaces. Ultimately, our findings highlight the alarming implications of HyperDegrade-enabled Flush+Reload attacks for the security of real-time systems. To mitigate potential risks, we suggest multiple strategies for enhancing system security, including the adoption of immutable memory models, stricter access controls for page mappings, and the implementation of regular memory integrity checks. To further raise awareness about memory attacks, we have established a dedicated webpage for tracking and demonstrating such attacks on various operating systems. The notion of a twisted virtual knot can be seen as a relaxed version of classical twisted knots. This relaxed version permits diagonal moves that are prohibited in the context of twisted knots. However, certain diagonal moves are beneficial as they allow for the simplification of a twisted virtual knot. In this study, we define a move called the "longer diagonal move" which can be applied to twisted virtual knots within a specific type of twisted knot called the untwisted Whitehead double. This twisted virtual knot variant is then introduced as a way to extend the braid-like structure known as the untwisted Whitehead double. Additionally, the longer diagonal move is utilized to demonstrate that this twisted virtual knot variant is equivalent to a classical twisted virtual knot. The untwisted Whitehead double remains an isolated example to date, as it is not possible to apply the longer diagonal move to any other variant of the twisted virtual knot known so far. A key aspect of cooperative decision-making among agents with varying objectives and capabilities is selecting tasks that are beneficial to the group as a whole. The distribution of task difficulties can significantly influence the decision-making strategies employed by agents. This research examines two common distributions of task difficulties: exponential and power-law distributions. Our findings indicate that decision-making approaches based on probability and utility maximization can lead to undesirable consequences, such as the avoidance of challenging tasks and prioritization of easy tasks to the exclusion of others. To address this issue, we propose two alternative decision-making policies: one gives each agent a set of tasks with equal chances of success, and the other designates the most challenging task for completion. Both approaches promote a more balanced selection of tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability and benefits of these policies in specific scenarios involving cooperative decision-making. Our approach to task assignment can be combined with existing algorithms, resulting in more efficient solutions, as evidenced by our experimental data. This research is relevant to various cooperative decision-making scenarios, including grid, multi-agent, and network formation games, and can be adapted for use in settings like electrical power distribution and transportation systems. The underlying theory and algorithms developed here can also be applied to human-driven systems, such as education and sports, where cooperation among diverse entities is beneficial for the group as a whole. This research was conducted as part of the MSIT program at Carnegie Mellon University, with additional support from the National Science Foundation under grant number IIS-1636936. In the context of vertical federated learning, users share unique portions of their data to train a joint model. We investigated private protocols that combine user contributions with emphasis on security. We developed two attack strategies, one analyzing model updates and the second targeting protocol privacy measures, to test the resilience of these protocols. Using vertical federated learning for spam detection, we trained a logistic regression model using user submissions. Our analysis showed that, despite protocol precautions, it's possible to identify user data, accurately predict their classifications, and even replicate the spam filter with a small degree of precision. Furthermore, we found a connection between the precision of these attacks and the protocol's privacy standards. We propose a new protocol that incorporates data encoding to enhance privacy protection, demonstrated in experiments using real-world data to train a gradient boosting model. This resulted in a decrease in prediction precision for both spam classification and user data identification, indicating its effectiveness. We also found a connection between encoding and a increase in training time, but found a sweet spot where a compromise between efficiency and security is achieved, showing that careful consideration of protocol parameters is necessary for efficient and secure vertical federated learning. We have publicly available code and data for reproducibility on our website. We have submitted our novel protocol for publication as well as our code and data to a separate repository on our website. Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF) have been proposed to speed up kernel methods by using a subset of RFFs, which are then further reduced in number. Researchers have demonstrated that PRFF surpass both RFF and the original kernel in terms of both the number of features required and predictive performance. The underlying idea behind PRFF involves selecting a subset of RFFs that are closest in value, which leads to a reduction in the number of features needed and helps avoid the leakage of sensitive information. In order to facilitate the nearest neighbor search needed for this method, a data structure known as a ball tree was employed. The benefits of PRFF were then demonstrated in kernel mean squared error regression and classification under two different regimes, in addition to achieving the optimal rate of feature dimension reduction in stochastic gradient descent. The code associated with the research is now openly accessible on a public repository hosted on GitHub. The underlying technique was also applied to a real-world instance of collaborative filtering, resulting in a lower mean absolute error when compared to RFF. The relationship between PRFF and the nearest neighbor search method they are based on was also thoroughly examined. The process of network fragmentation becomes increasingly complex as it's influenced by the size of avalanches, which are sudden shifts in node status, experts believe. To uncover the details of this interplay, researchers developed a mathematical model that incorporates the principles of network vulnerability and the spread of status changes. By analyzing this model in a highly simplified form, scientists discovered a critical point where the network's sudden shift from a state of fragmentation to complete breakdown occurs. Furthermore, research revealed that the size of avalanches plays a significant role in the formation of 'frozen landscapes' – stable network configurations that result from single node removals. In fact, the exact number of avalanches required to convert one network configuration to another can be any real number, demonstrating the intricate relationship between avalanches and network fragmentation. Finally, researchers found that the statistics of avalanches remain largely unchanged, mirroring the patterns observed in real networks, which exhibit self-similarity on every scale. This self-similarity is characteristic of 'fractal' structures that display the same patterns at different scales, as seen in mountain ranges and tree branches. This similarity in structure becomes visible when viewing the sequential changes of a network over time, rather than its static configuration. This new understanding of network dynamics is comparable to the concept of 'river landscapes' – a theoretical model composed of interconnected rivers that flow and change in response to external forces, yet retain their core structure. This 'river landscapes' model, in turn, is analogous to a mathematical formula known as the 'Kadashausky model', which has distinctive 'earmuffs' patterns in its structure. This 'earmuffs' shape can be observed in the specific arrangement of avalanches that occur in networks that have a particular property called 'hyperbolic structure'. This property is characterized by a unique distribution of distances between nodes that resemble a specific pattern known as a 'triangular structure', where every node is connected to every other node in its vicinity, akin to the arrangement of stars in the Orion constellation. This property is exhibited by various real networks, including financial relationships between companies and social connections between individuals. This means that the dynamics of these networks are driven by the same fundamental rules that create the 'river landscapes' structure, which in turn is influenced by the same principles that shape the 'earmuffs' pattern found in hyperbolic structures. This interplay results in networks that are resistant to changes, but once they do change, they shift suddenly and completely, as seen in a phenomenon known as a 'phase transition'.

XL-MIMO systems suffer from limited channel inversion root cause issues, hindering the scalability of sparse channel inversion. To address this challenge, NOVR-XL prioritizes user selection and allocation based on a novel sparse similarity metric, ensuring that only users with similar sparse structures communicate with each other. Furthermore, NOVR-XL allocates a sparse identifier to each user and employs a sparse matching algorithm in the random access phase. As a result, NOVR-XL reduces the random access delay, increases the system capacity, and decreases the system's energy consumption. The precise mechanisms involved in the early stages of disk evolution, where
small structures or gaps form and protoplanetary disks shut down, remain
subject to debate. Observations from the Herschel Space Observatory and the
Spitzer Space Telescope reveal a multitude of disks featuring gaps, and the
construction of the James Webb Space Telescope will likely yield more detailed
images of these intricate patterns. A computational model is presented, which
examines the dynamics of a 10-year old, 0.25 solar mass disk, powered by a
low-mass stellar primary with a rotational velocity of 1.2 km/s. A vast ring
structure was discovered in the near-infrared and mid-infrared spectra of this
disk, and the location and width of this ring are accurately replicated by the
computational model. The model also predicts the presence of a solid, dustless
inner region, which can provide a potential location for planetesimals to
formulate, thus contributing to the theory that small structures in protoplanetary disks are essential for the formation of planetesimals. The current model
exhibits an inner void with a radius of 1 AU, and this void is surrounded by
two massive ribbons with a width of 4 AU, and these ribbons are responsible
for the creation of the gap, in addition to the presence of a vast, dense
disk-based dust distribution in the outer regions. The model also reveals the
presence of a massive, solidary disk-based dust distribution in the outer
regions, and it is proposed that this could be the source of exoluminous
phenomena, such as comet-like objects, and the construction of future
high-resolution space telescopes will be capable of verifying this hypothesis. 
The computation model is also utilized to examine the effects of external
influences on the disk, such as the presence of a binary companion, and it is
determined that a companion with a mass of 0.1 solar masses, and a separation of
10 AU, is sufficient to replicate the ring structure observed in the spectra of
this particular disk. 
It is proposed that the construction of future high-resolution space telescopes
will enable the examination of the inner regions of the ribbons and the void,
in addition to the possibility of verifying the hypothesis that the solid, dust
less inner region can contribute to the formation of planetesimals. It is also
suggested that a binary or a binary-like system could be a crucial factor

A new version of the MacNayle--Kunheve energy density functional, dubbed BigApple D1, is presented, which is derived from a microscopical Hamiltonian consisting of the Gogny interaction through a Gutzwiller approximation and a Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov calculation. BigApple D1 yields a nuclear matter equation of state in excellent agreement with that obtained from the Gogny Hamiltonian and features a robust incompressibility of 216 units of density, which is a key factor in accurately predicting the properties of infinite nuclear matter. This new functional demonstrates notable improvements over its predecessors in predicting the properties of open-shell nuclei, particularly in regards to the rotational band and the magnetic rotation phenomenon. Our study employs BigApple D1 to investigate the collective rotation in even-even rare-earth nuclei across a wide range of mass numbers. A comparative analysis is conducted with two other energy density functionals, LYD1 and SDI, in predicting the energy spectra of the ground state, $2^{+}$ state, $4^{+}$ state, and $0^{+}$ state in nuclei characterized by highly deformed rotational behavior. A statistical evaluation of these predictions is carried out using a set of criteria that prioritize a functional's ability to simultaneously accurately predict multiple properties. This evaluation leads to BigApple D1 being the top-ranked functional in the study, with a particular emphasis on its ability to predict the energy differences between successive rotational levels with high precision. A comparative analysis is also conducted with two other parameters, namely the fission fragment mass distributions in neutron-rich actinide and rare-earth nuclei and the beta-plus delayed gamma proton emission in highly neutron-rich proton emitters. Our study indicates that BigApple D1 exhibits a high level of predictability in a vast range of nuclear matter scenarios. This new energy density functional is referred to as BigApple D1-Y1 in the Yonsei version, which is obtained by multiplying BigApple D1 by a factor of one in the density term in the density-dependent term. BigApple D1-Y1 is utilized in predicting the properties of exotic nuclei across a wide range of mass numbers. We investigate the performance of Molmer-Sorensen gates across different frequency settings to determine their potential for universal entanglement generation in optical lattices formed by one-dimensional ion chains. The analysis focuses on the robustness of Molmer-Sorensen gates within fluctuating environments and highlights the benefits of tailored designs in achieving prolonged entanglement accumulation. By analyzing various frequency configurations and their effects on the Michelsen criterion, we identify an optimized scenario where the 95% confidence interval for the duration of validity meets or exceeds 100 seconds in the presence of stabilization pulses. In this scenario, a specifically designed Molmer-Sorensen gate maintains a minimum entanglement coefficient (r) of 0.01 for a chain of 20$^{1}$ ions within a 200-KHz frequency range. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this robust gate protocol can be effectively combined with a variety of auxiliary pulses, including a three-body effective interaction simulator, a pair of binary effective beamplumps, and a dynamical phase controller, all while maintaining the required level of frequency robustness. This finding paves the way for universal entanglement generation and the effective incorporation of three-body interactions in ion chains via optical dressing. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/entanglement-robust/MR-robust-entanglement-generation. This analysis allowed for the prediction of exact electronic states and possible experimental observations in this material. For instance, replacing chlorine with oxygen was found to induce a phase transition in GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$. Experimental verification of the predicted results is feasible with the help of advanced techniques like angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. This study highlights the unique features of GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ and its potential for contributing to a deeper understanding of complex many-body phenomena and Dirac electrons within cubic materials. This knowledge could also aid in the discovery of other materials exhibiting similar properties. This research was conducted as part of a PhD project at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids in Germany. This doctoral thesis builds upon research presented in several scientific papers co-authored with colleagues. This study delves into the theoretical examination of a complex material's electronic properties through the application of a combination of approximation methods. This analysis yields a clear understanding of the exact electronic states present within the material and offers predictions for both its experimental behavior and possible composition modifications. This study focuses on the theoretical analysis of a specific material, a cubic compound called GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$.
