Reconstructing a three-dimensional face from images under various lighting conditions and facial poses is a complex task. Previous methods typically train separate models for pose-independent and pose-dependent components, thus requiring substantial data and complex architectures. In contrast, a novel framework, the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet), decouples the 3D face reconstruction process into two independent, yet aligned representations. By doing so, it redefines the task as two separate, yet interconnected problems: estimating a pose-independent face proxy and predicting a pose-dependent displacement vector from the input image. By leveraging shared features and employing a self-aligned technique, the two components learn from each other, thus achieving a more accurate and efficient reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses the state-of-the-art performance in multiple metrics for 3D face reconstruction. Additionally, the model's ability to generalize to new poses and lighting conditions is showcased through ablation studies. Moreover, the evaluation shows that the proposed face proxy serves as a reliable face identity representation for biometric recognition tasks, outperforming existing methods in both the performance and parameter efficiency. In particular, the proposed model achieves the lowest error rate in the challenging FMEL protocol, thus indicating its potential for real-world biometric applications. The code for the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network is available at https://github.com/zhanglei2019/SADRNet.

Researchers analyzed the effects of large negative values of the Bardeen potential's fluctuations in the context of single-field inflationary models. By re-examining the relationship between the Bardeen potential and the scalar power spectrum, they discovered an area of parameter space where the Bardeen potential takes extremely large negative values. This phenomenon is particularly noticeable when the nearly scale-invariant scalar power spectrum is combined with specific slow-roll conditions. A combination of an ultra-slow-roll phase and a phase of pole-like instability in the sound speed can also produce the desired effect. To study this phenomenon, they created a new variable that exhibits a linear relationship with the Bardeen potential and Bardeen potential fluctuations. This new variable allows for a more intuitive understanding of the Bardeen potential's fluctuations. Additionally, it was possible to reinterpret the conditions for generating large negative values of the Bardeen potential's fluctuations as the generation of extremely large negative values of the new variable's fluctuations. This new variable also enables the identification of specific features in the power spectra of the Bardeen potential and its fluctuations, which can be crucial for reconstructing the Bardeen potential from its fluctuations in simulations of post-inflationary scenarios. In summary, this new variable provides a valuable tool for analyzing the effects of extremely large negative values of the Bardeen potential's fluctuations in the context of single-field inflationary models. Furthermore, this variable can be applied to any model of inflation and serves as an essential quantity in its own right, offering valuable insights into the power spectra of the Bardeen potential and its fluctuations. Quantifying a tree's depth structure has implications for various fields, including genetics, information retrieval, and economics. This study examines average deepest node counts in ordered trees and marked ordered trees under standard ordering. By employing the gamma function, we obtain closed-form expressions for the expected number of deepest nodes in both tree variants. For standard ordered trees, the result shows the average number of deepest nodes is $\frac{2}{\phi}$, where $\phi$ is Euler's number, compared to the 4-unit interval, and this contrasts with the 2-unit interval commonly used in similar studies. For marked ordered trees, we find the corresponding value to be $\frac{4}{\pi^2}$, demonstrating that the ratio of the interval used affects the estimated deepest node count. Our research also explores the relationship with a similar problem involving the root distance in standard ordered trees. This work builds upon previous studies, particularly those by Pittel in 1987 and 1990, as well as Schlecht-Ohlsen in 2011. Our approach differs from their analytical approaches but yields congruent results. This study is also related to the root distance problem solved by Janson and Schlecht-Ohlsen in 2011, and it shares a common aspect with the work of Pittel in 1987, which involves the use of the gamma function to calculate negative binomial distribution's expected value. This type of calculation is also utilized in the recent work by Janson, Krueger, and Ruschendorf in 2019. This research can be extended to examine the distribution of the maximum branch length in planar maps, which is a more complex problem. This study was initially published as part of the research for Janson's 2011 Ph.D. thesis. This work shares a common aspect with the research on the sum of uniform variables with range restrictions, which was examined by Janson, Krueger, and Ruschendorf in 2019. This type of problem is analogous to finding the distribution of the maximum branch length in planar maps, which is another unresolved issue. This research can be seen as an expansion on the work done by Janson, Drmota, and Valier in 2005 and Janson in 2011, who examined the sum of uniform variables with range restrictions defined by polynomial equations, which is a more general problem. This general problem includes tree-related problems as special cases. This type of problem is also known as conditional uniform variables or hidden uniform variables

This approach leverages the knowledge that the model's parameters will eventually become obsolete, and applies it to an over-parameterized linear model. As a result, the method reduces the infinite data to a compact, time-sensitive summary, and facilitates efficient training on just the accessible parts of the data. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach through numerical tests and comparisons with standard methods. In power grids aimed at reducing carbon emissions, storage facilities with risk-tolerant capabilities can generate substantial economic benefits. To capture the value of adaptable storage, a mathematical model has been developed which takes into account the uncertainties of temperatures and electricity prices in urban areas. By analyzing data from Texas and California, the research reveals that storage resources are risk-averse and tend to perform poorly in extreme conditions. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that storage facilities are able to adjust their performance in response to changing risks and reveals that risk-adaptation enhances the economic advantages of storage for energy grids. Moreover, the research shows that appropriate policy designs, such as feed-in tariffs and renewable portfolio standards, influence the risks that storage resources face and, in turn, affect the profitability of these facilities. By factoring in risk-adaptation and storage performance in extreme conditions, the model shows that the benefits of energy storage in the Western United States and Texas are significantly greater than previously estimated. Consequently, there is a pressing need for grid managers and policymakers to consider the risks that storage resources face and the benefits of adaptable risk profiles when planning and designing low-carbon energy systems. In fact, the research reveals that storage facilities that can adapt to changing risks can provide up to twice the amount of services to the grid than non-adaptive storage resources. Additionally, the study highlights that appropriate policy designs and risk management strategies are crucial for inducing risk-adaptation in storage resources and, in turn, enhancing the economic advantages of these facilities for the grid and the environment. In the context of the Western United States and Texas, the research presented suggests that a combined policy that includes capacity payments, renewable portfolio standards, and environmental hedging could encourage risk-adaptation in storage resources and, as a result, provide up to $1.5 billion in additional economic benefits to these energy systems by the year 2025. Moreover, the research indicates that storage resources with risk-adaptation capabilities will continue to offer significant economic benefits to energy grids worldwide as the frequency of extreme weather events rises with global temperature increases. A computer simulation of an Earth-like atmosphere was run on a computer to see what circulation patterns would develop. The simulation was set up to represent a slow-rotating planet with an irregularly shaped axis, and it included computer codes that mimic the effects of clouds and temperature differences on atmospheric circulation. A prominent storm pattern emerged on the simulated planet, mirroring the behavior of baroclinic storms observed on Mars. Notably, the simulated storms displayed the same asymmetrical characteristics and circular flow patterns found in the Martian atmosphere, specifically the polar vortex and the massive storm around the equator. Notably, dust storms on the simulated planet behaved similarly to those on Mars, forming near the polar ice caps and migrating towards the equator during the local spring. The simulation also revealed that the polar ice caps on the simulated planet melted during the local summer, releasing large amounts of water into the atmosphere and accelerating global warming. The model showed that this feedback loop accelerated the melting of the polar ice caps on the simulated planet, transforming it into a more Mars-like state. The simulation lasted for 120 years, during which the polar ice caps on the simulated planet shrank by half. The study suggests that a baroclinic storm cycle could play a crucial role in the geologic history of Mars, particularly during the time when the planet had ice caps and polar ice polar caps. The simulation showed that a baroclinic storm cycle could create a global dust storm that blocks sunlight and cools the planet, causing the polar ice caps to grow again. The study also found that the timing of the polar ice cap growth and the baroclinic storm cycle might be offset by several years, creating a self-sustaining cycle. The research simulated a range of different solar luminosities and atmospheres on the simulated planet, finding that the baroclinic storm cycle and the polar ice cap growth and shrinkage form a self-sustaining cycle of warming and cooling. The study suggests that this cycle of warming and cooling might explain the patterns observed in the Martian geological history, particularly the recurring periods of dust storm activity and polar ice cap growth. The research also found that the baroclinic storm cycle can create a habitable environment on the simulated planet for a limited period, specifically during the transition from a warm phase to a cold phase. The study found that this window of habitability is short-lived, lasting only a few decades, but it might be sufficient for life to adapt and thrive before the planet becomes uninhabitable again. To overcome these difficulties, researchers are exploring the use of donor atoms in silicon, which can serve as quantum bits, or qubits. By carefully positioning and adjusting these donors, scientists aim to create efficient two-qubit gates by leveraging their sensitive energy levels and long-range electrical connections. To achieve this, various donor configurations are simulated using a comprehensive model that incorporates electrical connections and quantum properties. These simulations demonstrate how adjusting the energy levels of single-qubit donors can lead to efficient two-qubit gates, and show that tuning the energy levels of multiple-qubit donor arrays allows for multiple two-qubit gate implementations. Furthermore, the model is applied to an existing experimental setup to help interpret available data. Ultimately, this research provides a versatile tool for designing donor-based qubit arrays and exploring various implementation scenarios. To facilitate further study, the simulation data is made available online.

Theoretically, this Landau level should remain completely resistant to scattering, yet in practice, it seems to be affected by scattering processes, especially those occurring in quantum wells with a short carrier lifetime. Furthermore, by combining the results of both experiments, the team was able to demonstrate the distinctive characteristics of the zero-point Landau level and the limited impact of the Fermi level, as well as the direct application of the quantum Hall effect's edge state theory to a central feature. The discovery of the zero-point Landau level's behavior has significant implications for the understanding and manipulation of carrier scattering, as well as the edge state theory in the quantum Hall effect, which exhibits robust resistance oscillations at low temperatures in the absence of an external magnetic field. The absence of an external magnetic field allows for the direct investigation of the carrier scattering process itself, rather than it being indirectly measured through the edge states' resistance. The discovery of the zero-point Landau level's behavior also allows for the investigation of carrier scattering in the quantum well's ground state, in a regime described by a linear disorder class that is distinct from the usual Al'tshuler-Aronov-Spivak disorder regime. The discovery of this new disorder regime provides a unique window into the investigation of the quantum well's ground state carrier scattering process, which is influenced by the presence of a superlattice. In a collaborative learning environment where multiple agents work together, accuracy and trustworthiness are crucial factors. We present a social learning framework called FedHeD, which is a decentralized version of federated learning and incorporates a hierarchical evaluation method to build trust among the agents. FedHeD distinguishes itself from other federated learning frameworks through the incorporation of agent hierarchy, where agents with higher prestige are more influential in model updates and evaluations. Furthermore, FedHeD determines the trustworthiness of each agent based on accuracy, identifies potential malicious agents, and includes detection mechanisms for internal data breaches. We conducted experiments using both clean and tampered datasets on three datasets, Mobiplex, Cifar10, and Sent120, and the results showed that FedHeD achieved higher accuracy levels on Mobiplex and Cifar10, and comparable levels on Sent120, when compared to the conventional federated learning approach. Additionally, FedHeD demonstrated robustness in securing against data breaches, as it successfully detected all the nodes compromised in the experiments with tampered datasets. We also validated FedHeD's scalability by conducting large-scale experiments on 1024 nodes with clean datasets, and the results showed that FedHeD could efficiently handle large datasets with high accuracy levels. We have also included the code for the hierarchical evaluation method and the trust score calculation, which can be found at the following link: https://github.com/ali-khoshkhooseligh/HED. We believe that FedHeD has significant potential applications in various collaborative learning environments, such as smart cities, healthcare, and the internet of things, among others. Researchers have observed top quark production in proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Electron Collider (LHC). Top quarks were identified through the decay of $B$ hadrons, which were selected using a displaced vertex topology tag. The cross-section for this process was determined and found to be in agreement with predictions from quantum chromodynamics. A comparison of different theoretical predictions showed variations, with the most accurate model matching the observed data. A comprehensive analysis was conducted with all available top quark cross-section predictions, incorporating both leading-order and next-to-leading-order calculations with and without next-to-leading-order corrections. These predictions were then utilized in a study of the theoretical uncertainties affecting the cross-section measurement. Additionally, the distribution of the number of $B$ hadrons produced in association with a top quark was examined and found to align with predicted patterns. A further analysis was performed to assess the prospects for detecting rare exclusive processes at the LHC, particularly at the Large Hadron Electron Collider. This led to the development of an optimized strategy for identifying the process of producing a single top quark, which is characterized by the presence of a displaced vertex with two $B$ hadrons and a significant missing transverse momentum value. Precise and efficient database performance depends on accurate initial parameter settings. This challenge becomes more significant in dynamic systems like cloud databases, which vary in structure and size. Existing solutions focus on learning from historical errors to produce better results in similar, subsequent situations. In contrast, a novel framework called APER (Accuracy-enhanced Parameter Initialization in Databases through Reinforcement Learning) aims to achieve high accuracy from the start. APER employs RL to train an initializer agent to produce optimal initial settings across diverse database scenarios. Unlike previous solutions, it achieves success in its very first attempt, without needing access to actual database error data. Instead, the agent uses the feedback from the database's response to its initial settings. This enables it to master various databases with different contents, similar to how humans learn. In a comprehensive evaluation, APER demonstrated the ability to provide accurate initial settings in a wide range of situations, without relying on prior experience. Moreover, it was found to excel in dynamic database environments, where other solutions struggled to adapt. APER's outstanding performance was observed regardless of whether the associated database contents were present, incomplete, or varied in structure. In addition, the proposed framework was found to be highly efficient, capable of handling a large scale databases with ease. In comparison to other solutions of similar kind, APER was found to require significantly less training, database data, and computational resources. In summary, APER offers a groundbreaking approach to database performance improvement through accurate parameter initialization, based on its unique dynamic learning properties. This makes it an highly promising solution for various applications in the cloud databases domain. Furthermore, the development of APER also led to a novel evaluation method for other initializer algorithms and related solutions in the field. This evaluation highlighted the critical importance of accurate performance in the first execution attempt in cloud databases, without the need for actual error data. In addition, APER's efficiency in handling big data, low requirements for training and computational resources, and the diversity of databases it can handle with ease, all make strong case for its widespread adoption. To understand how private information might be inferred from a learned model, researchers typically analyze the privacy risks using the private gain of a trained model compared to the original dataset. Determining this risk involves calculating the privacy loss, a concept that, due to the complications introduced by data graph interconnectivity, requires significantly more computational time for highly interconnected data sets under differential privacy. In our analysis, we outline two novel methods for efficiently calculating privacy loss on general data graphs by utilizing a combination of topological properties. Our approach leads to a substantial decrease in computational time, especially when analyzing large, highly interconnected data sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical implications of our methodology by conducting an extensive set of experiments utilizing real-world data sets and pseudo-real-world generated data sets. In these experiments, we observed a direct correlation between data graph interconnectivity and privacy loss, which, in turn affects the private gain of a differentially private model. Our research was motivated by an examination of a specific neural network learning task, but our methodology is applicable across various machine learning tasks that incorporate differential privacy. Our study highlights the significance of considering data graph interconnectivity in machine learning, which, in turn, affects various aspects, including sampling, preprocessing, and learning from datasets. In recent years, Knowledge Distillation has become a prominent technique for creating highly efficient neural network models with limited parameters. The traditional approach involves training a lightweight student network alongside a corresponding large teacher network, with the student's predictions being treated as soft labels. However, this method does not fully take advantage of the knowledge embedded in the distribution of the teacher's soft labels. A novel architecture called TSD addresses this limitation by utilizing multiple intermediate student networks of varying sizes, which are trained by corresponding teacher networks and knowledge distillation processes, with the ultimate goal of creating a highly efficient neural network model. By leveraging the knowledge from the distribution of the teacher's soft labels, TSD achieves superior performance on a range of benchmarks, with results showing significant improvements in classification accuracy across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. The code for TSD has been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. As part of the research, a new regularisation technique called Knowledge Diffusion Regularisation is introduced, which facilitates the convergence of multiple neural network models during the knowledge distillation process. The regularisation technique has been successfully applied to traditional knowledge distillation scenarios with compelling results. Absorption of highly saturated light can result in a significant deviation from the typical Lamb dip profile due to the interplay of absorption, scattering, and photon recoil. We theoretically examine the shape of a dip in absorption spectra, considering both the saturation level and the number of light interactions with a system. By applying this analysis to an idealized scenario with a two-level atom, we derive an expression for the dip lineshape, taking into account the effects of photon recoil, the saturation level, and the light frequency spectrum. This expression can be used to predict the behavior of more complex systems with multi-atom interactions and various initial states. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach by comparing it to results from the quantum master equation, which provides a more detailed but less general description of the same scenario. Furthermore, we discuss the connection to a recent experiment that observed a narrow dip in the absorption of highly saturated light by a rubidium gas, and outline possible directions for future work. If the dip is sufficiently narrow, the dip lineshape can be determined solely from the knowledge of the scattering phase space, rather than the explicit time-evolution of the system. We also highlight the potential utility of this approach for protecting fragile quantum states from dissipation induced corruption. If a system is coupled to a bath through a highly saturated classical channel, we show that our approach can be used to develop strategies for safe quantum information processing. If the dip is wide, the usual linearized description of dissipation becomes relevant, but with different assumptions it can also be derived from our expression for the dip lineshape. We refer to this derivation as the ``dressed'' linearized dissipation theory. This new theory yields the same results as the standard linearized theory in its domain of applicability, but it also provides predictions for the behavior of the system in the regime where the linearized theory typically fails. We believe that this new theory has value in its own right, and could be particularly useful for simulating the dynamics of systems in the regime of correlated fluctuations of the system and bath variables, which is typically modeled using non-linear effects of dissipation. We demonstrate the utility of this theory by comparing it to an exact solution for a quantum phase noise model that was studied in a recent experiment. The classification of jamming transitions is characterized by an analysis of critical exponents. Recent studies on frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming have revealed distinct exponent configurations, suggesting these jamming states constitute distinct universality classes. To further clarify the relationships between these states, researchers have been attempting to compare their exponents with a particular focus on determining if frictional shear jamming and frictionless isotropic jamming share the same universality class. A comprehensive understanding has yet to be achieved due in part to the unknown relationships between face-centered cubic and hexagonal close-packed jamming configurations. A new study on frictional jamming induced by shear in face-centered cubic jamming configurations has shed new light on this issue. Faced with the challenge of identifying the universality class of FCC jamming, researchers discovered it transitions to HCP jamming through a first-order phase transition, and also found that FCP and isotropic jamming share the same universality class, both exhibiting the same critical exponents except for one key exponent. A notable finding from this study is that the gap in one of the exponents, when changing from 3D to 2D, increases with friction. A novel state of matter referred to as frictional shear jamming was previously introduced in a letter form and is further validated in this paper. A distinctive feature of this state is the presence of a cusp-shaped singularity in its phase diagram, and has been confirmed not to be a interface transition but rather a bulk phase transition. A thorough analysis in this study reveals that the mechanics of frictional shear jamming is governed by the same exponents as those found in frictionless isotropic jamming. The term universality class of frictionless isotropic jamming is thus too broad, consisting of at least two subcategories of universality classes, namely frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming. The challenge of distinguishing these two subcategories was initially met with the development of a novel model referred to as the harmonic spring model. The mechanics of the harmonic spring model exhibit the same exponents as frictionless isotropic jamming in 3D, however in 2D it was found to be uncertain about its universality class due to the presence of multiple phase transitions within the model. The development of the harmonic spring model led to a deeper understanding of the relationship between face-centered cubic and hexagonal close-packed jamming configurations, revealing that the former is induced by shear in the latter configuration. The widespread use of Google Web search as a primary source of information necessitates public sector professionals being aware of algorithmic biases influencing Web search results. This study examines the effects of five user-agent switches on Google's search engine algorithm's ranking of search results, revealing significant variations in ranking. The magnitude of these differences is substantial, with some results ranked as high as 10th being shifted to the top of the list, and others ranked as low as 29th being moved to the first position. The variability in ranking is so great that it can't be explained by safe answers or biased results being distinguishable. Consequently, public sector professionals should consider the potential risks of relying on Google search as a source of information for official purposes, and consider developing policies to address this issue. Furthermore, educators should incorporate media literacy that takes into account the inherent biases of Google search. Moreover, both public and private sector organizations should be aware of the potential risks of relying on Google search for critical decisions, and consider alternative search engines for official use. Suggestively, a simple algorithm is proposed that could be used by search engines that aim to reduce the impact of user-agent based bias. Finally, future research directions are proposed, including the investigation of mobile search results being biased, and the analysis of search engine bias based on geographic location, browser type, and other factors. Additionally, recommended practices for search engines that prioritize fairness, and potential policy interventions, are also discussed. A TeV-scale muon collider, with its capabilities of producing highly energetic particles, can facilitate comprehensive studies of various particle production processes, complementing existing research at the Large Hadron Collider. This paper delves into a detailed examination of hadron production in a muon collider, specifically focusing on the creation of light quarks, gluons, and heavy quarks within protons and nuclei. Our study involves conducting comprehensive theoretical calculations for relevant hadron production processes and comparing them to predictive models used in experimental research. Furthermore, we outline strategies for extracting precise information about parton distribution functions from data obtained through hadron collisions at a muon collider. A proposed sampling method called rCASPR leverages the symmetry of circular collimation to produce non-uniform point-spread functions, resulting in a reduction in point-sampling time while maintaining comparable image quality compared to conventional linear sampling. The rCASPR technique achieves this improvement without requiring control over the detector or real-time data processing. A study using Monte Carlo simulations compared rCASPR to linear sampling over a range of sampling patterns, rotation speeds, and tissue types, revealing a 2-fold decrease in point-sampling time while maintaining comparable NEC times and image contrast scores. Moreover, rCASPR demonstrated point-spread function variations across different sampling locations, offering potential benefits for improving SPECT image reconstruction. The method's simplicity makes it suitable for various single-photon tomography technologies. The results obtained suggest rCASPR's potential for enhancing the efficiency of existing SPECT systems and providing valuable data for further research in image reconstruction. The rCASPR code is available online for the modification and testing by the scientific community. The proposed sampling strategy was tested using data from a phantom scan conducted on a clinical SPECT system. The data is also publicly available for comparison and validation purposes. The rCASPR algorithm is suitable for various applications, including but not limited to, clinical use, research in image reconstruction, and educational purposes. The code can be utilized for other circular sampling techniques by adjusting the radial sampling patterns. The proposed method enhances the understanding of the relationship between sampling technique, point-spread function, and image contrast, facilitating educational uses in the fields of medical physics and engineering. The rCASPR code can be used within the GATE simulation platform, a widely-used Monte Carlo simulation framework for medical imaging and radiation therapy. The code is compatible with various input file formats commonly used in medical imaging simulations, including but not limited to ANSYS, G4ELASTICPRECONV, MATHEMATICA, TEXT, and XML. The proposed sampling method was tested using real data from a phantom scan conducted on a clinical SPECT system designed by General Electric Healthcare, model Infinia. The paired-permutation test is a statistical method used to analyze differences in datasets from before and after an intervention. This test's exact implementation is computationally intensive, prompting the development of Monte Carlo approximation algorithms. However, the Monte Carlo method may yield unreliable results if set to an excessively high precision level. To address this limitation, an exact algorithm has been created for the paired-permutation test, featuring a more efficient permutation sampling approach known as conditional sampling. This new algorithm compares similarly to the Monte Carlo approximation method even at a relatively low precision level the test, offering enhanced performance when comparing two datasets via permutation tests. When comparing multiple datasets, it achieves a significant speedup. When comparing a single dataset to a predefined threshold, it matches the Monte Carlo method's speed. The algorithm's efficacy has been demonstrated through the analysis of real-world datasets and commonly used test types. Its code has been integrated into popular statistical software packages. Moreover, a command has been added to the R programming language for easy access to this algorithm. The algorithm's core, known as the condys library, is also accessible from Python via R's remote procedure call feature. A comparative study showed that this exact algorithm, when conducting the paired-permutation test on a large dataset, could be up to 20 times more efficient than the Monte Carlo approximation method when striving for a 0.01 percent precision level. When comparing multiple datasets, it can be up to 60 times more efficient. When comparing a single dataset to a predefined threshold, it can be up to 10 times more efficient. This algorithm has practical applications in various fields, including neuroscience, economics, and sports research. A concrete example can be found in the analysis of a real-world dataset from a renowned economics research project. This algorithm has a versatile nature and can be utilized in a wide range of statistical analyses involving permutation tests. Moreover, the condys library includes multiple test types, such as the paired-permutation test, the unpaired-permutation test, the permutation test for multiple comparisons, the permutation test for time series datasets, and the exact algorithm for the minimum spanning tree. This algorithm's efficiency can be further leveraged by utilizing high-performance computing, as demonstrated by the successful analysis of a large dataset comprising 15 million data points. This research examines the recent deregulation of the shipping industry, specifically the 1997 abolition of shipping cartels in Japan. We analyze the resulting changes in freight rates and shipping quantities for the Kanto region's scrap paper trade. Initially, significant and persistent effects from the deregulation are observed. However, other factors like a global supply shift, the 2008 financial crisis, and increased port competition eventually overshadow the initial impacts. We also compare the results with a control group of non-scrap paper trades in the Kanto region and a national panel of Japanese trades. The results show that shipping quantities increased and freight rates decreased for all trades in the Kanto region, but only scrap paper trades experienced this change before the 2008 financial crisis. A shift in shipping patterns is also evident for the regional trades. Furthermore, the effects of the deregulation on shipping quantities and freight rates in Japan are similar to those in the Kanto region, except for a notable shift in shipping quantities for the national trades that occurred in 2011. We also investigate the effects of the 2011 tsunami on the shipping industry in Japan. The findings suggest that the increased shipping distances and decreased shipping quantities observed in 2011 were primarily caused by the tsunami rather than the 1997 deregulation. We also examine the breakdown of shipping cartels for individual trades and find that this breakdown was delayed for some trades, including the scrap paper trades in the Kanto region and Japan as a whole. We analyze the time it took for shipping quantities to respond to price changes in a generalized ARDL framework. The results indicate that the response of shipping quantities to price changes increased and the adjustment speed accelerated for all trades in the Kanto region and Japan following the deregulation. However, the speed of adjustment was slower for the regional trades than the national trades. We also compare the adjustment speeds of the regional trades with different shipping distances and find that the trades with shorter shipping distances experienced faster adjustment speeds. Additionally, we examine the effects of the 2008 financial crisis on the shipping industry in the Kanto region and find that the increased shipping distances and decreased shipping quantities observed in 2008 were primarily caused by the financial crisis rather than the 1997 deregulation. We also examine the effects of the 2011 tsunami on the shipping industry in Japan. Technological advancements have significantly increased the accessibility of technical indicators and historical stock price data for machine learning models. This access has led to a rise in research on using these data sets to forecast stock movement. A critical aspect of this research involves dealing with the high dimensionality of indicator data, which can compromise model efficiency. In response, dimensionality reduction techniques have been applied, but the effectiveness of these methods depends heavily on the parameters employed and the specific indicators used. Additionally, the relationship between the indicators and future stock movement remains poorly understood. An innovative approach involves utilizing the Baggel graph-based dimensionality reduction technique to explore the relationship between technical indicators and future stock movement. This method enables the selection of the most relevant indicators and the identification of indicator combinations that exhibit distinct patterns of behavior. In studying historical stock price data for a range of companies, our research reveals that indicators can be grouped based on either their direct correlation with past stock movement or their independence from historical behavior. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate the feasibility of predicting stock movement with a chosen set of indicators and suggest that the most reliable indicators are those reflecting the long-term relationships with past stock movement. In contrast, indicators exhibiting non-linear relationships with past stock movement are less reliable in this capacity. In the stock market context, the temporal invariance of relationships presents a complication. Thus, models trained on data from one time period may not be effective for another period. To address this challenge, our research involves training multiple models on consecutive periods of stock data and evaluating the performance of these models on successive time frames. Our results indicate that the most stable indicators are those reflecting long-term relationships with past stock movement, while the most volatile are those reflecting non-linear relationships with such past movement. In addition, our study reveals that the performance of models is inversely proportional to the dimensionality of the indicators employed. Ultimately, our innovative approach to exploring the relationship between technical indicators and future stock movement contributes to our understanding of this complex dynamic and provides a practical solution for addressing the high dimensionality of indicator data sets. This approach is applicable to predictive models using technical indicators and historical stock price data. In our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach using a conventional machine learning model and demonstrate the temporal invariance of the relationships discovered. Our research also includes an examination of the relationship between the performance of models and the employment of technical indicators in conjunction with fundamental data. In this assessment, we discover that the indicators reflecting short-term relationships with past stock movement are the most informative in this context. Our experiments cover multiple companies

The Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) share the same underlying structure, with the Higgs sector of both theories being driven by identical set of operators after eliminating the electroweak symmetry. As a result, the HEFT and SMEFT are equivalent descriptions of the same phenomena, with a direct relationship between their coefficients. In the context of double Higgs production, we have determined the corresponding coefficients of the SMEFT from the HEFT ones. Furthermore, we have derived explicit expressions for these correspondences at the level of tree-level Feynman diagrams. In addition, we have validated our results against the global fit of the SMEFT parameters to the available data, employing the relevant tools for this purpose.

The context of metric expansions in general relativity is clarified, and a novel method to facilitate the analytical treatment of cosmological perturbations through successive non-relativistic corrections is presented. A particular "pre-non-relativistic" coordinate choice allows for an analytical expansion of the metric, effectively re-expressing the perturbations in terms of non-linear combinations of the non-relativistic variables and correction terms. This substitution simplifies the derivation of successive approximations and directly yields the relative weights of various non-linear effects in scalar perturbations. As a practical application, a multidimensional cosmological parameter space can be explored through the use of Taylor series expansions around a non-relativistic reference frame, making it possible to analytically handle the effects of deviations from a non-relativistic scenario on cosmological observables. This approach is particularly useful for analyzing the impact of non-relativistic bulk fluctuations on electromagnetic probes and is demonstrated by investigating the influence of relativistic quantum effects, non-linear scalar perturbations, and bulk non-relativistic velocities on the cosmic microwave background and various observable quantities in the late universe. Furthermore, this method can be easily extended to the study of fundamental quantum gravity effects in non-relativistic bulk fluctuations. A comparative analysis of different expansion approaches is also discussed, along with the pre-non-relativistic frame's suitability for a wide range of cosmological contexts. This work is relevant to various research contexts, including those described in the papers listed below. Researchers from the University of California and Harvard University conducted an experiment to determine the drag experienced by a cylindrical object as it moves through a granular bed, using a camera system to analyze the movement and a laser sensor to measure the surrounding grains. Driving the cylindrical object at a constant speed allows scientists to study drag in a state of equilibrium, and by varying the speed, they can examine both the start and stop phases of movement. A dimensionless drag coefficient was calculated from the data, and by combining it with other research, a new formula was derived to predict the drag experienced by a cylindrical object during movement through a granular bed, known as the drag phase diagram. This diagram shows how drag varies in different situations, and includes information about the direction of movement, the speed of movement, and the depth of movement. Ultimately, the study aims to contribute to a broader understanding of the complex interactions between movement and friction in granular environments. Additionally, the experiment's data reveals a notable phenomenon known as stick-slip drag, and the factors that influence the drag experienced by the cylindrical object include the size of the grains, the shape of the object, and the speed at which it moves. The research was conducted by undergraduate students at the University of California, and the results have implications for fields such as geology, physics, and engineering. The study's findings can be applied to areas like the movement of rocks, the flow of sand, and the behavior of granular materials, and it also contributes to a broader category of studies known as stick-slip dynamics. The experiment's design is highly visual, making it suitable for undergraduate project work, and the resulting data can be used to teach students about topics such as dimensionless analysis, phase diagrams, and statistical data processing. The study's findings have been presented at academic conferences, and the results have been published in a peer-reviewed journal. This study examines the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow, denoted by $p_T$-dependent $v_3$, in two colliding systems via the ratio of $v_3$ to $v_2$. A notable similarity is observed between these ratios in both the LHC and RHIC energy ranges for selected hadrons like $\pi$, K, and P. A functional form that incorporates the ratio of $v_3$ to $v_2$ is used to compare semi-analytical hydrodynamic models and empirical parameters extracted from existing data. Both models demonstrate a self-similar pattern characterized by a single parameter, the Knudsen number, which is indicative of collisionality in ultra-relativistic QCD plasmas. Furthermore, both hydrodynamic models predict the $p_T$-dependent ratios exhibit self-similar patterns across various energy levels, allowing for a direct comparison between the ratios in different energy settings through use of an updated energy-dependent Knudsen number. This comparison leads to an adjustment of previous estimate and confirms that ultra-relativistic QCD plasmas behave according to $\text{Kn} \propto \sqrt{s_{NN}}/p_0^2$, where $p_0$ is $2$ GeV in the current analysis. Additionally, both models indicate that hadron species influence the $p_T$-dependent ratios by mean transverse momentum rather than transverse momentum spectra directly. Therefore, a modified ratio that normalizes by mean transverse momentum is proposed and evaluated using existing data and simulations. This evaluation shows that hadron species are determined by mean transverse momentum rather than transverse momentum spectra in ultra-relativistic QCD plasmas. This paper outlines the rare decay research that the LHCb experiment at CERN plans to conduct in 2015-2016, utilizing 9.5 inverse picobarns of 2 TeV proton-proton collision data. Rare decay observations, particularly rare B-meson decays like B^0_s to mu+ mu- and B^0 to mu+ mu-, are the focus of this study. A previous B^0_s to mu+ mu- measurement made by the LHCb collaboration already exists, but the planned analysis aims to enhance the current understanding by several aspects. With an expected 1.6 times improved signal significance, this study hopes to achieve the following: assess the B^0 to mu+ mu- decay rate with an accuracy of 0.2 picobarns^-2, determine the CP-violating phase beta_s with an accuracy of 3.5 degrees, and evaluate the B^0 to J/psi gamma decay branching ratio with an accuracy of 5%. Moreover, this research will also enable the evaluation of rare decay processes involving charm hadrons, rare tau and kaon decays, and photon-induced interactions. A new LHCb Monte Carlo simulation incorporating realistic rare B-meson decay descriptions will be utilized in this study. Additionally, this research will involve developing new analysis methods for addressing experimental challenges associated with multiple Pion production in rare B-meson decays. Furthermore, this study will also involve the cross-validation of rare decay process predictions made using theoretical models, such as the Standard Model with Euclidean lattice gauge theories, the Improved Standard Model, the Slepton-Neutral Higgs Sector, the Two-Higgs Doublet Model, and the Scalar Sector, as well as the derivation of implications for these models following the observation of rare B-meson decays. This research will also result in the publication of various related papers in other disciplines mentioned above. This rare decay research at the LHCb experiment is expected to provide valuable insights into the behavior of subatomic particles and help scientists better understand the fundamental nature of matter and the universe. This knowledge will also help scientists in their search for new physics phenomena beyond the current understanding of the universe. The modification takes advantage of the accuracy enhancement offered by recent MP extensions and focuses on the FGMRES iteration, a fundamental method in iterative linear solvers. Theoretical analysis indicates that the composite FGMRES iteration achieves a higher precision than standard FGMRES by a factor of 2, which is especially significant in critical precision settings. Experimental results on various sparse matrices highlight the advantages of CFGMRES in terms of both the number of iterations and solution accuracy when employing different precision levels. Furthermore, the composite scheme is applicable to multiple iterative solvers and linear system types, demonstrating its versatility. The research highlights the efficacy of the composite FGMRES iteration in resolving precision-related issues affecting iterative linear solvers. Accurate organ model registration is crucial for enhancing surgical outcomes and reducing side effects. Although registration algorithms are highly effective, intraoperative data is often marred by noise, complicating precise model alignment. This study aims to address this challenge by introducing a robust feature extraction method utilizing the intrinsic properties of laparoscopic temperature images. Initially, a heat map is created to highlight areas of temperature change and suspicious tissue growth, representing the organ's surface. Next, a geometric filter is applied to remove extraneous information and produce a simplified model features, which are then compared to the original model to identify alignment opportunities. A robust algorithm is employed for actual alignment, and the results are validated in a phantom study and five real laparoscopic surgeries. The findings demonstrate a high registration accuracy even with noisy data, outperforming a widely used algorithm in various scenarios. Furthermore, the proposed feature extraction method is comparable in accuracy to using noisy data directly for registration. In addition to surgical applications, this research presents innovative techniques for extracting meaningful information from temperature images, which could be valuable in other medical contexts, such as oncology. The proposed framework has been made available open-source on GitHub. The current study focuses on a specific surgical procedure, but the methodology is versatile and could be adapted for other situations involving the registration of preoperative and intraoperative data. In recent years, self-supervised flow estimation has made significant progress, largely relying on temporal consistency constraints to learn optical flow from video data. Nevertheless, determining the exact amount of occlusions in a scene remains a difficult task for the network, leading to inconsistent estimation results. Our research builds upon the temporal consistency based method, optical flow in the wild, and introduces a new regularization term inspired by the work on image self-consistency. This additional constraint encourages the network to produce consistent flow estimates between adjacent frames, utilizing a minimum amount of occlusions as a reference, which is easily determined as zero. Through extensive testing, our optimized flow estimation model demonstrates improved performance on publicly available evaluation metrics. Furthermore, our experiments indicate that the proposed regularizer effectively reduces flow estimation inconsistencies caused by occlusions. Our code is available online at the following repository: https://github.com/zhengxiaoyi/OFTC-ISRC. 

In the process of testing, our approach encountered an issue where the network overestimated occlusions in scenes with moving objects and small displacements between frames. Our analysis revealed that the flow estimation model produces inconsistent results for regions with moving objects due to the limited range of the hyperbolic distance function used to compute optical flow. This realization prompted us to exchange the traditional hyperbolic distance function for a more flexible one, namely the Euclidean distance, which allows for a broader range of possible flow fields. Our modified approach demonstrates improved performance on the task at hand. Moreover, our results show that using Euclidean distance yields comparable performance to hyperbolic distance when evaluating the accuracy of optical flow estimates, as defined in the Sintel protocol. Nonetheless, our approach requires special consideration when computing the gradient of the Euclidean distance, which is not a straightforward operation due to the indirect path of computation. Our solution to this challenge entails expressing the Euclidean distance as a function of the norm of the difference vector, which facilitates the computation of the gradient via the chain rule. Our code for this research is available online at the following repository: https://github.com/zhengxiaoyi/OFTC-EUDD. 

Our approach to flow gradient computation was found to provide a more intuitive understanding of how the Euclidean distance function can be utilized to compute the gradient via the chain rule. In recent years, Spiking Neural Networks have demonstrated superior performance and efficiency, and their potential as general-purpose classifiers has been explored. Our research develops a 5-class classifier called SNN-Tree, consisting of a hierarchical structure with increasing precision, inspired by nature by utilizing distinct classification categories. SNN-Tree surpasses the current record for the most precise spiking neural network by achieving 98.17% accuracy on MNIST, and its energy consumption per operation ranks the lowest among comparable SNNs implemented on real hardware. Our novel model also outperforms the current benchmarks for classification tasks, including MNIST (97.53%), EMNIST (94.33%), and Cancer Subtypes (96.57%). Our unique spiking algorithm allows for a wide range of learning rates and our simulator exhibits near-linear scaling when handling large datasets. Our real hardware implementation on the Memristor-based NeuroShuffle Architecture shows a 10 times reduction in power consumption compared to a high-performance GPU. Our model and algorithm have been made available online for public use. Our research paves the way for the creation of efficient and accurate spiking neural networks that can be applied to a wide range of classification tasks. The quark masses are calculated for various degrees of polarization and Fermi surface anisotropy, and the equation of state for the matter is determined from the quark distribution functions. A study of the energy density, pressure, and heat capacity of the matter is also conducted. The calculation considers the impact of a linear and quadratic magnetic effect on the masses of the quarks. The behavior of the matter is compared with strange quark star models under the constraint of the Einstein mass limit. The relationship between the neutron star radius, central density, and the anisotropy of the Fermi surface is examined. The minimum mass of the stars is also calculated for different constants of the interaction and the anisotropy of the Fermi surface. The effects of a linear or quadratic magnetic effect on the masses of the quarks are investigated. The calculation of the magnetic effect considers the charge neutrality condition and the presence of massive electrons in the neutron star model. The results indicate that a strong magnetic field causes the polarization of the quark matter to decrease, which in turn leads to a decrease in the mass of the stars. The maximum allowed density also decreases with an increase in the anisotropy of the Fermi surface. The combination of a quadratic magnetic effect and the anisotropy of the Fermi surface leads to an increase in the minimum mass of the stars. An even-2-factorable cubic graph is defined by having a 2-factor whose components are cycles of even lengths and being connectable to those components via single edges. This work demonstrates that any cubic graph with a 2-factor containing only cycle components of specified lengths can be modified into an even-2-factorable cubic graph through the addition of a specific number of edge-connections and vertex-connections. This process is achieved without increasing the number of connections required and without affecting the specified component sizes. Furthermore, an algorithm is provided for accomplishing this transformation. The main argument is supported by two key results. First, for any given positive integer n, it is possible to prove that there exists a value Nn, such that for any cubic graph with a 2-factor consisting of cycle components of lengths 2, 4,..., 2n, it is possible to connect those components with single edges to produce an even-2-factorable cubic graph. Additionally, an algorithm is offered to accomplish this even-2-factorable transformation in polynomial time, with respect to its input size. Second, it is shown that for any given positive integers m and n with 2 ≤ m < n, there exists a value Mn such that for any cubic graph with a 2-factor consisting of cycle components of lengths 2, m, 4,..., 2n, it is possible to connect those components with single edges to produce a 2-factorable cubic graph. Moreover, an algorithm exists to accomplish this 2-factorable transformation in polynomial time, with respect to its input size. The concepts used in this work are based on the properties of a 2-factorable cubic graph that were established by Gyárfás, Ruszitzki, and Szárnyasi in 2010 and the properties of an even-2-factorable cubic graph that were discovered by Fidler, Haggmark, and Kral' in 2011. The results presented in this work were first established by the author in his Master's thesis that was supervised by J. Kral'. The algorithm provided in this work was inspired by the ideas presented by Brouwer, Havel, and Schrijver in 1982 and by the ideas presented by Haggmark in 2013. The relationship between the values Nn and Mn was discovered by the author during the preparation of this work. The values Nn and Mn were both found by the author using a computer program that was created based on the ideas presented by Brouwer

The rapid evolution of web attacks necessitates robust system call filtering for safety-critical web applications. Existing solutions are often tied to low-level programming, but what about applications written in interpreted languages like PHP and Python?  To address this challenge, we developed Timeloops, a lightweight Linux filter that automatically blocks malicious system calls for interpreted web applications in PHP, Python, and Joomla.  By analyzing the source code of popular web frameworks, Timeloops prevents system calls from reaching the kernel and detects potential vulnerabilities in applications.  We demonstrated Timeloops' effectiveness by integrating it with Apache and Nginx web servers and conducting system call injection experiments on vulnerable applications.  Our results show that Timeloops effectively blocks system calls for over 70% of interpreted web applications and prevents the execution of common attacks like RCE and file leaks.  Moreover, Timeloops incurs a minimal performance overhead of approximately 1% on real-world workloads.  We have publicly available Timeloops implementations on GitHub and encourage web developers and server administrators to utilize this secure system call filtering solution.  Additionally, we provide a predictive model to determine system call safety for interpreted web applications based on source code analysis, demonstrating the feasibility of assessing an application's safety prior to deploying it.  We also discovered multiple system call injection vulnerabilities in popular web frameworks like Apache Struts, Django, and Flask, and reported these findings to the relevant project maintainers for correction.  We believe our system call safety assessment approach can be applied to various web application frameworks and help ensure the security and reliability of web services.  We plan to expand Timeloops' predictive capabilities to assess vulnerabilities in new web frameworks and provide recommendations for improving system call safety.  We also invite server administrators and web developers to contribute to Timeloops and the safety assessment models for a free and open community benefit. This study examines the observability inequality for a population model that combines the Euler--Lagrange equation and the transport equation. We aim to establish an inequality measuring the observable quantity, which reflects the distribution of a population within a geographic area, based on incomplete data collected from limited observation points. We have developed this observability estimate in two forms: the first form determines the time required to acquire sufficient data to monitor the population's extinction risk, while the second form enables us to pinpoint the exact time when the population will go extinct. Furthermore, we have numerically demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by simulating the spread of a population subject to a decline rate and presenting the corresponding data observed at various points. Additionally, we have explored the implementation of this method on a two-dimensional geometric area known as the torus. The associated numerical results are comparable to those obtained through the classical inverse problem approach. The observability inequality can be further applied to ensure that the population does not become extinct in a given period by managing its decline and distribution. Moreover, we have analyzed the possible outcomes for the population size based on its initial state and a management strategy that affects the Euler--Lagrange equation, thereby providing a framework for managing the population effectively through the observability inequality. This approach can be adapted to model the spread of other dynamical systems subject to decline or evolution in a geographic area. We have also considered a random distribution of the population and validated the accuracy of our method by conducting numerical experiments on various geometric areas known as spheres and toruses. We have explored the application of this method to a linear transport equation and a nonlinear transport equation known as the Burgers equation. We have explored the effectiveness of our approach on a geometric area known as a sphere with a surface covered by observation points with different densities. This study was published in the journal Mathematics, 2023. The associated code can be found in the repository Observability Inequality 2023. We analyze the strategic decisions made during game stoppages in soccer by examining the choices players make following a foul committed against them. To do this, we used a Markov Decision Process model incorporating variables such as the opponent's distance from the goal, time remaining, and score. Our data source consisted of 1,502 game stoppages from a Premier League match, analyzed in detail to compare the potential rewards for actions like shooting, passing, or kicking the ball to restart play. Our findings show that, in many situations, players are more likely to kick the ball to a teammate rather than shoot, often choosing to pass even when shot would be a better option. This behavior can be attributed to the risk of failing to score and suffering retaliation from the opposing team, and may also reflect the limited shooting skill of certain players. Ultimately, our model indicates that players undervalue shooting in situations where they have a clear shot on goal, and this preference influences their decisions during game stoppages. Our research also offers an improved model for evaluating shot opportunities and provides insights for coaches and players on optimizing game strategy. Furthermore, our analysis provides a framework for assessing the impact of kickoffs and free kicks in soccer, including the value of taking shots, and the rewards associated with successful passes and kicks. This is particularly useful for applying machine learning techniques to analyze game dynamics and evaluate player behavior. Our approach can be applied to other sports featuring game stoppages and kickoffs, and provides a method for evaluating shot opportunities based on game variables, offering a level of objectivity missing from subjective assessments. Our model can be used in simulations, and also offers possibilities for optimizing game strategy in real-time, and even for designing defensive strategies aimed at minimizing the rewards associated with kickoffs and free kicks. A key issue in time-domain full waveform inversion (TD-FWI) arises from the eikonal equation's breakdown when using time-domain wavefields, particularly when source and receiver locations coincide or near each other, causing singularities in the slowness model. This paper presents an approach using the phase function in the frequency domain to bypass this problem and avoid the challenges associated with time-domain wavefields. By taking the real part of the complex frequency domain wavefield, we develop an inversion method tailored for the modified eikonal equation in the frequency domain. Additionally, this TD-FWI technique can handle the source signature's removal and the Riemann surface associated with the complex frequency domain phase function. Numerical examples demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in both smooth and complex geophysical settings. The results indicate that the proposed method yields accurate and robust slowness models, even under conditions with near-source singularities. The proposed technique's flexibility in incorporating the source signature without additional processing is also highlighted. The need for the frequency domain approach to avoid the time-domain wavefield's singularity-related issues is further emphasized by the results showing the time-domain counterpart of the proposed method failing to produce reliable slowness models in the near-source environment. The potential of this frequency domain TD-FWI method in real-world applications is also discussed. The code associated with this research is available online at https://github.com/rtsh/tdfwi. The proposed algorithm's potential advantages and limitations are further explored in the following text. The proposed frequency domain TD-FWI technique leverages the extended phase space framework, which enables the source signature's incorporation into the inversion process. The frequency domain approach allows the eikonal equation to be defined without the source signature-related singularity issues encountered in the time domain. The robustness of the proposed method in the frequency domain is demonstrated by applying the TD-FWI to a model with near-source singularities. The proposed method's performance is compared to the time-domain FWI implementation on the same model, revealing the time-domain method's failure to produce reliable slowness models in the near-source environment. The frequency domain FWI results show the proposed method's ability to recover the correct slowness model even in the presence of near-source singularities. The robustness of the frequency domain FWI is further demonstrated by applying the method to a model with a thin layer of low velocity contrast. The asymmetric noisy voter model on a lattice represents an exemplary system for examining competition between different species. Depending on the level of asymmetry and noise, several equilibrium outcome can result from the competition between two species, including the coexistence of both species, the extinction of one species, or one species dominating the other. Our study focuses on the asymmetric noisy voter model on a random regular graph of any given degree, where we demonstrate the existence of a coexistence phase where both species thrive, as well as the exact conditions under which one species will triumph over the other. Our data from simulated noisy voter model runs match the predicted patterns of both the coexistence and the exclusive equilibrium outcomes. We also compare the noisy voter model results with those generated from the asymmetric opinion dynamics model, which exhibit equivalent outcomes in the same-degree setting. The key factors determining the model's equilibrium state involve the level of noise, the asymmetry between opinions, the model's noisy or conditional version, and the model's underlying network structure. The results we derived using random regular graphs also apply to random connection tables that ensure a specified minimum connection probability between any two given degrees. The exclusive equilibrium state outcomes are determined by the difference in the connection probabilities between the two species, which we refer to as the species bond asymmetry. The determination of the exclusive equilibrium state outcomes relies on the bond asymmetry parameter, the level of noise, and the level of asymmetry. The coexistence phase outcome requires the bond asymmetry parameter to be below a certain threshold, which is defined as a function of the level of noise and the level of asymmetry. The determination of the outcomes in the asymmetric noisy voter model and the asymmetric opinion dynamics models involve the application of the invasion convolution equation and the invasion convolution equation with a success function, respectively. The solutions to these equations involve the solution to a system of nonlinear equations, which can be further reduced to a single nonlinear equation with one variable, as well as the application of the mean-field approximation on a random regular graph. The conditions under which the coexistence phase or the exclusive equilibrium state outcomes arise can be determined by examining the roots of the nonlinear equation, which are compared to a reference value that depends on the level of noise and the level of asymmetry. The determination of the reference value involves the solution to another nonlinear equation, which can also be reduced to a single nonlinear equation with one variable, as well as the application of the mean-field approximation on a random regular graph. This system enables the transfer of both data and energy to users and serves as a platform for TFIET array applications. By developing TFIET array capabilities, the required time and energy for computing specific TFIET configurations can be determined, yielding an algorithm for sampling TFIET ensemble states. Additionally, the TFIET array is shown to generate TFI ensemble states that are highly similar to those produced by the original Yang-Mills model, yet with a significant reduction in the time and energy needed. This leads to a TFIET array implementation for sampling TFI ensemble states and associated variational ansatze for the Yang-Mills field, with an accompanying code available online. This code includes TFIET array simulations, corresponding TFI ensemble states, and associated variational ansatze, all of which can be readily modified by users. Furthermore, this proposal paves the way for an integrated quantum processing and transmission device that leverages a TFIET array in both a variational ansatz capacity and a data transmission role, enabling both the efficient sampling of variational ansatze and the transfer of data and energy to users in a single integrated setup. The study presents simulations of electrostatic phase plates under conditions similar to those found in scanning transmission electron microscopes (STEMs). The design of the plates includes various fill-factors and distinct pixel patterns. The models account for the precise alignment of the plate's pixels with the STEM's scan probes. The simulations examine the relationship between the probe size, current density, and design features of the phase plates. The results indicate that the most efficiently designed plates correspond to those with the highest fill-factors that match the STEM's scan parameters. The optimal design is found to produce the smallest probe sizes and highest current densities. The study further shows that the shape of the probe current density peaks directly correlates with the shape of the phase plate's pixel pattern. The most favorable conditions produce a probe current density peak width of 0.17 pm and a current density of 0.85 nA/pm. The research demonstrates the importance of precise design of phase plates in achieving the desired performance in STEM instruments. The results provided can serve as targets for the development of optimized phase plate structures using advanced techniques in electron beam lithography. The study emphasizes the potential for significant improvements in the performance of existing STEM instruments through the replacement of their phase plates. The research also highlights the challenges faced in determining the exact conditions of existing phase plates, which would be necessary for calculating the exact performance improvement achievable with a new plate. The latter would require precise knowledge of the production process used for the existing plate, which is typically unknown due to the lack of accurate metrology tools for post-process analysis of the complex nanostructures found on phase plates. The development of such tools is essential for the field. The study suggests possible approaches for determining the conditions of existing phase plates, including the simulation of the lithography process used to manufacture the mask, combined with the post-process analysis of the mask's nanostructures, followed by the simulation of the electron beam interaction with the probe-forming optics and the phase plate. The ultimate goal of this multi-step simulation would be to calculate the exact performance of the existing STEM instrument, which in turn would enable a precise comparison with the performance of the new phase plate and the calculation of the exact performance improvement achievable with its installation. The research further highlights the potential challenges faced in the simulation of the exact conditions of existing STEM instruments due to the complexity of accurately determining the precise conditions of the probe-forming optics and the phase plates. The study emphasizes the potential benefits of developing advanced metrology tools for post-process analysis of the complex nanostructures found on phase plates and the probes

This study examines the orbital stability of solitary anharmonic oscillators in one-dimensional systems with the anharmonic oscillator represented by a variable coefficient damped wave equation. We first establish the existence proof of solitary solutions under certain conditions and then investigate their orbital stability through the Rayleigh quotient technique. Furthermore, we compare the anharmonic variable coefficient damped wave equation with the anharmonic damped wave equation and the Euler-Lagrange equation, leading to a system of integral equations that enable us to determine the variance of solutions and thus conclude the orbital stability of solitary solutions. We also investigate the effects of anharmonicity and coefficient variability on the variance of solutions. Additionally, we numerically investigate the anharmonic variable coefficient damped wave equation using a pseudo-spectral finite difference method. The results show that the anharmonic variable coefficient damped wave equation exhibits a wider range of solution variances compared to the anharmonic damped wave equation, demonstrating the capability to recover lost energy. The ability of the anharmonic variable coefficient damped wave equation to recover energy is further validated by comparing the cumulative energy change of the two equations over time. The numerical examples presented involve exact solutions of Korteweg-de Vries, Sine-Gordon, and nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger equations. The results also demonstrate the capability of the variable coefficient damped wave equation to recover exact solutions of the Korteweg-de Vries equation and the Sine-Gordon equation through the inverse scattering transform method. The numerical examples are validated using the method of exact solutions, the conservative law, and the conservative flux function. The results obtained also meet the requirements for proving the global existence and the orbital stability of solutions to the initial value problem of the variable coefficient damped wave equation. The numerical examples presented can be extended to higher dimensional systems.
