To extend the Chern-Simons gravity theory to include a rotating hairy black hole, we examine if the entropy of these black holes matches the entropy produced by pure Chern-Simons gravity. To achieve this goal, we analyze a specific type of Chern-Simons gravity theory with a vector field and modify the theory to include a rotating hairy black hole within its solution space. By using the entropy formula associated with Chern-Simons gravity, we compare the entropy of these rotating hairy black holes to the entropy generated by pure Chern-Simons gravity. To validate our findings, we verify that our analysis complies with the laws of black hole thermodynamics. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between our modified Chern-Simons gravity theory and the original Einstein-Chern-Simons gravity theory. Furthermore, our study includes an examination of the causality of the theory in question. In our research, we also explore the relationship between the entropy of rotating hairy black holes and the heat capacity of the theory. Our results demonstrate that the heat capacity of the theory becomes negative at a specific temperature, indicating that the theory loses causality at that temperature. Our research also reveals that the loss of causality is accompanied by the breaking of the entropy bound, the divergence of the entropy density, and the heat capacity becoming negative. Our study further shows that the temperature at which the theory loses causality is governed by the AdS black hole entropy density bound, the Hawking-Page phase transition, and the heat capacity of the theory. Our research also reveals that the AdS black hole entropy density is directly proportional to the number of vector fields in the Chern-Simons gravity theory. Our study includes an examination of the relationship between the AdS black hole entropy density and the heat capacity of the theory, as well as the ratio of the heat capacity to the AdS black hole entropy density. Our research demonstrates that these ratios remain constant across different spinning states of the same Chern-Simons gravity theory. Our study also compares the entropy of rotating hairy black holes in the context of Chern-Simons gravity with the entropy produced by pure Chern-Simons gravity, with results showing that the difference between these two entropies is directly proportional to the square of the spin parameter of the black hole. Our research further reveals that this proportionality holds for spinning black holes in both five and seven dimensions. Axial ax estimation is typically more precise than lateral estimation and is critical for reconstructing strain images. A novel approach uses a convolutional neural network in spectral domain elastography, targeting the real part of the axial displacement complex value. Experimentation on realistic numerical phantom data and clinical breast tissue elastography cases shows the accuracy of axial displacement estimates rivals traditional methods. Furthermore, the proposed technique yields comparable results to state-of-the-art methods on in-vitro object and breast tissue data, often with a computation time five times faster. Computational efficiency enables application to real-time imaging, while the technique's accuracy is unaffected by elastogram noise. A version of the code is available at the Elastika repository. The proposed technique leverages the CNN's ability to distinguish frequency components, facilitating axial displacement estimation with minimal training, even on limited data sets. The technique's utility in breast elastography is further highlighted by the minimal impact of tissue intensity on estimate accuracy. The technique's Axial-Phase-Unwrapping-Net architecture is also introduced, along with suggested design guidelines for developing neural network-based elastography algorithms. The code is designed to be highly customizable, allowing end-users to easily generate and test various models for different elastography applications. The research underpins the feasibility of using neural networks in real-time ultrasound elastography, paving the way for a two-factor BPA-based approach to improve estimate precision. The proposed technique's limitations are also discussed, along with potential solutions, such as developing a separate network for lateral estimation or incorporating additional information from raw ultrasound data. The potential of the technique in the context of shear wave elastography is also explored, along with the proposed Axial-Phase-Unwrapping-Net architecture's suitability for this application. The code release aims to foster collaboration and drive innovation in neural network-based ultrasound elastography algorithms. The research has implications for improving elastography accuracy in various medical applications, including breast, liver, and prostate elastography. The technique's computation time makes it suitable for real-time ultrasound imaging, while the code's customization options enable users to explore and evaluate different neural network-based elastography algorithms for specific use cases. The purpose of this research is to present a new approach for evaluating the correctness and safety of software designed using logical pseudocodes. This assessment involves comparing the designed system with the intended specifications and guaranteed properties outlined in the pseudocodes, ensuring the pseudocodes' correctness and safety. This evaluation method is made possible by the development of a specialized formal verification framework, which includes a declarative specification for the pseudocodes as well as a set of tools for the verification process. This framework has been successfully applied to the validation of multiple existing protocols and system designs, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach. Furthermore, the differences between the predicted and actual behavior of the designed system provide valuable information that can be utilized in the verification process itself, enabling the discovery of pseudocodes' errors as well as the generation of test cases, especially those that are counterexamples. This approach has a particular advantage when combining the verified pseudocodes with machine learning models, as it offers access to the underlying data and counterexample analysis, thus potentially leading to the improvement of existing protocols and the creation of new ones. This research was motivated by the analysis of existing logical pseudocodes and reveals a wide range of errors, including inconsistencies within the pseudocodes themselves, failures to meet promised guarantees, and unforeseen consequences of designed systems, as well as the discovery of possible counterexamples among assumed premises, showing that the verification of pseudocodes is crucial in ensuring the reliability of designed systems and sometimes reveals previously unknown issues with established protocols. This research was further applied to the evaluation of two prominent machine learning models, namely the training data they rely on and the assumptions underlying their decisions, demonstrating the feasibility of this approach in real-world applications. This research was also applied to the detection of attacks on sensitive information in two prominent protocols, demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in ensuring the safety and security of designed systems and machine learning models. We develop a one-pass coreset creation algorithm for the $k$-means clustering issue, producing a compact representation of size directly proportional to $k$ and $d$ for a dataset with $n$ points in a $d$-dimensional space. This coreset enables the efficient solution to the original problem by employing a one-pass deterministic algorithm on the reduced dataset. The coreset construction process involves examining multiple branches of an abstract tree associated with the input points. Each branch corresponds to a distinct clustering configuration and is chosen based on a relevant criterion. We leverage the concept of a centroid tree to inform the coreset construction, which in turn is based on the Euclidean distance structure. This coreset generation algorithm enjoys a theoretical guarantee, as it produces a coreset with a size that is polynomial with respect to the parameters $k$, $d$, and the maximum distance between any two points, and which is sufficient to support the solution to the original problem with a factor of polynomial overhead. This achievement is significant because, for a one-pass creation process, the size of the coreset must be at least proportional to $k$ and $d$. This result extends and improves upon our previous findings for one-dimensional data in [Ioannidis et al., 2020] and provides the first known instance of a one-pass coreset creation algorithm for clustering in multi-dimensional spaces. This algorithm's efficiency is compared to alternative approaches by exhibiting the impracticality of attempting to replicate the guarantee achieved in one dimension in higher dimensions. This coreset creation algorithm serves as a key component for an efficient approximate $k$-means clustering protocol to be described in a subsequent paper. This protocol leverages the coreset in conjunction with a one-round multi-party secure computation protocol to enable the solution to the original problem with a polynomial factor overhead, without requiring any private information about the individual points among the participants. This achievement is significant because, for a one-round protocol, the required private information would otherwise be at least proportional to $n$ among the participants. In large-scale grid worlds, efficient decision-making is crucial for agents navigating and identifying hidden targets. A key challenge arises from the vast number of possible world states, posing a significant obstacle for real-time decision-making through exhaustive examination of the grid. To address this issue, the concept of superstates can be introduced, representing a subset of world states that behave identically and provide a coarser representation of the environment. A model-based approach is presented that utilizes superstates for forward planning, yielding a grid-based extension of the Pursuit-Evasion Problem with Partial Knowledge (PEPCK). A novel grid partitioning method is introduced, tailored to the superstate framework, which facilitates the efficient update and expansion of the superstate grid. Experimental evaluations comparing different state partitioning strategies across various knowledge structures and scales demonstrate the advantages of superstate representation in the Pursuit-Evasion Problem. The proposed approach is particularly beneficial in crowded grid worlds with partial knowledge, as it offers several benefits over traditional PEPCK, including improved efficiency in target identification and evasion path planning. The superstate grid framework additionally provides a versatile tool with applications in related domains, such as the Pursuit-Evasion Game in Partially Known Grid Worlds. The proposed algorithm is evaluated using various metrics including the number of node expansions, target identification time, and evasion path length, and is found to offer several advantages over the original PEPCK algorithm. The superstate grid framework is versatile and has been tested in multiple domains including the Pursuit-Evasion Game in Partially Known Grid Worlds, the Narrow River Network Flow Problem, and the Traffic Management Problem in Grid Worlds. The algorithm has been made available for download on the author's webpage. The code was developed using MATLAB version 7.10.0.499 (R2010a) and executed on a Linux platform with an Intel Core 2 Duo processor and 12 GB RAM. The average execution time for each experiment is approximately 5 minutes. The code size is approximately 10 MB. The algorithm was tested using 21 different domain instances, with domain-specific parameters varied across different experiments. The algorithm includes several customizable parameters, which are summarized in the appendix. The algorithm has been validated to operate without errors in the tested domains. The algorithm includes a built-in error detection mechanism that flags any domain-specific programming errors. The algorithm has been designed to operate without user input during execution, with all necessary data loaded from external files prior to execution. By using a numerical PDF set popular in particle physics simulations, this research also compares the PDF corrections to those of the kernel at lower energies. When applying a single learned dynamics model across multiple reinforcement learning tasks, several challenges arise. Using a unified state representation can lead to conflicting training signals, causing the model to prioritize the most data-rich task and neglect the needs of others. Furthermore, employing a single model may result in dynamics being overlooked or misestimated for certain tasks, leading to subpar performance in tasks with extreme or unusual state-action distributions. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view dynamics model that represents and learns separate dynamics for each task using a task-specific state representation, which is shared across views to prevent overfitting. By utilizing a carefully designed regularizer, we ensure that the views cooperate in modeling the underlying dynamics, thereby avoiding the confounding of similar states and actions. The proposed model receives the action to take the system from one state to another as an additional input, which we believe is a novel contribution in its own right. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our multi-view dynamics model in multiple scenarios, including across different policy trajectories, real and simulated data, and in scenarios with both intrinsic and extrinsic rewards. Our approach outperforms comparable baselines in tasks like learning to navigate mazes and control a simulated robotic arm. Our code is available at https://github.com/kuangyang79/multi_view_dynamics.

This paper introduces a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which yields a theoretical sample posterior distribution. This achievement enables the utilization of posterior sampling in applications involving imaging. We prove that RCWGAN generates the same posterior samples produced by its optimal parameter, and further establish that RCWGAN incorporates the capability to classify conditioned data compared to unconditioned data. Additionally, we demonstrate in experiments involving both natural and synthetic data that RCWGAN surpasses its counterparts in terms of performance. This success is attributed to RCWGAN's capability to classify conditioned data, which contributes to a reduction in the mode-seeking issue it faces. This mode-seeking reduction facilitates RCWGAN in achieving superior results in comparison to traditional WGAN incurred due to conditioned data classification. This occurs specifically when the class is viewed as an additional feature, which adds to the dimensionality of the data distribution. This makes the task of RCWGAN even more challenging, yet it is capable of overcoming this difficulty. This challenging task is analogous to solving two separate classification and image synthesis problems with concatenated features, which results in RCWGAN achieving the lowest Fr\"{o}schteiner score among the compared methods in all experiments conducted. This score assesses the difficulty of a task that a model de facto solves in addition to its primary objective, which in this case is generating realistic samples. This generation capability is evaluated using the Improved Salience Inception Score, while the Fr\"{o}schteiner score itself is calculated based on feature extraction through a trained neural network and assesses whether a model can extract specific features from the data it was trained on. This is accomplished by comparing the accuracy of the model in assigning these features compared to a ground truth standard. This feature extraction ability is demonstrated to be applicable in real-world scenarios through the successful deployment of a customer feedback analysis system that leverages this ability to classify feedback with high accuracy. This means that the model is able to learn the implicit definition of a particular class from data, which is a complex multi-class classification problem, requiring the model to generalize effectively in order to accurately classify new instances of this class. This capability of the RCWGAN is further validated through the successful deployment of the customer feedback analysis system on a large scale, covering multiple product categories across different brands, with varying levels of success, as well as on text from social media, with comparisons to comparative methods conducted through the utilization of publicly available datasets, consisting of text classifications by multiple users. This validation is accompanied by a comparative analysis of RCWGAN with the comparative methods

This research examines the invariance properties of linear subspaces in fractional order systems. We define an approach to extend the concept of invariance to subspaces, similar to its application in integer order systems. A system is considered responsive to a input if its output is nonzero for a non-zero input within a specific subspace. We establish conditions for a system's subspaces to remain invariant when connecting systems in fractional order. These conditions are analogous to those in integer order systems and include the system's poles and zeros also being invariant. We also investigate the properties of a fractional order system's response to inputs from specific subspaces, referred to as its signature. This research provides examples and case studies of fractional order systems, including the Riemann Zeros, the Lorenz system, and a mechanical system with friction. We develop a method to determine a system's minimal representation while ensuring its subspaces remain invariant. This approach is comparable to the approach used for the system's state-space representation. We use the Matignon star product to represent fractional order systems. This research can be applied to the analysis of fractional order linear time-invariant systems that satisfy the conditions of stability and regularity. This research provides a foundation for extending its applications to systems that are delayed or of integer order in specific subspaces. This can be useful in the analysis of systems with fractional components, switched systems, and the dynamics of populations and networks. The quasi-periodic nature of human speech necessitates signal models that capture recurring patterns across various time frames. While recurrent neural networks have achieved high accuracy in speech generation tasks, their complex structure makes it challenging to interpret the learned representations. In contrast, a cascaded network, with a fixed filter bank and repeated applications of a simple spectral transformation, efficiently replicates recurring patterns across time frames. In this work, we present a cascaded neural network model that integrates a mel-based frequency analysis with a repeated application of a sinusoidal transformation, thereby learning a distance metric that diminishes over time frames. We believe this distance metric represents the temporal distance between speech elements, analogous to geographical distances in traditional multidimensional scaling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this model by achieving an accuracy of 75.1% in distinguishing utterances within the same time frame frame as 0.11, which is a 26.6% reduction in relative error compared to a recurrent neural network. This finding suggests that cascaded networks effectively capture recurring patterns in speech signals with a high degree of resolution. In addition to speech, this model also successfully generates other quasi-periodic signals like guitar music and walking patterns. In the process, we discovered an important issue with the current evaluation methods for neural network-based speech element detection tasks. We propose a new evaluation metric, the relative error of temporal distances, which provides a more accurate assessment of detected speech elements. This metric is applicable to the detection of speech elements in video data accompanying the paper, which can be found at the following link https://youtu.be/8s6s2O3RV7Q. This evaluation metric is versatile and can be used for the detection of speech elements in video data accompanying the paper, which can be found at the following link https://youtu.be/8s6s2O3RV7Q. This evaluation metric is applicable to detected speech elements in various modalities including video, which is illustrated in the accompanying video at the following link https://youtu.be/8s6s2O3RV7Q. Building on the foundation established in the paper where the bicategorical version of topological Hochschild homology (THHH) was first defined, this follow-up work develops the concept of shadows within a bicategorical framework. Initially introduced in the earlier paper, shadows in this context refer to a way to associate a bicategorical version of THH to any given bicategorical version of THH. The subsequent sections of this paper explore the relationship between shadows and the THH of bicategories, revealing that the THH of bicategories forms a part of the shadow of Asperk's bicategorical version of THH. The subsequent sections also examine the connection to the THH of monoidal categories, discovering that the THH of monoidal categories corresponds to the shadow of Berman's bicategorical version of THH. The final section of this paper presents the relationship between the THH of symmetric bicategories and the shadow of the THH of bicategories under the forgetful functor. The appendices to this paper feature detailed proofs of various statements made in the earlier paper on the bicategorical version of THH. The connection between the THH of symmetric monoidal categories and the shadow of the THH of bicategories is also explored in one of the appendices. The remaining two appendices provide a description of the THH of bicategories in terms of the cyclone construction and present the relationship between the THH of symmetric bicategories and the shadow of the THH of bicategories under the forgetful functor. The original paper on the bicategorical version of THH can be found in the journal Geometric & Topological Methods in Physics. VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) is a comprehensive audio classification dataset comprising 10 distinct categories of sound sources, encompassing both natural ambient sounds and synthetic artificial sounds. Comprising 10 classes and 49,300 classified 10-second audio clips, VGG-SS surpasses existing sound classification datasets in scope and diversity. Notably, it stands out from other datasets by including artificial sounds, thus offering a unique resource. When put through training, VGG-SS demonstrates superior performance compared to other sound classification datasets, including a 49.8% improvement in the mean class accuracy on the large-scale SoundStream dataset commonly used in an autonomous vehicle context. Moreover, VGG-SS exhibits a versatile nature, having been successfully applied in an autonomous vehicle context, a setting characterized by a constant stream of new sounds. The dataset and classification models have been made publicly available through the official website of the MMDSP research group. The research underlying VGG-SS has been accepted for presentation at the 2024 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP). This paper presents a novel neural network structure, the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which applies the concept of Lorentzian distance to graph convolution. Lorentzian distance is chosen because it aligns with the current standard method of representing hyperbolic graphs and offers a meaningful way to measure the similarity between neighboring graph patches. A key contribution of this work involves deriving an intuitive and efficient learning rule for Lorentzian graph convolution, resulting in the LGCN. When compared to existing hyperbolic GCNs, the proposed model significantly improves node feature representations. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the LGCN's performance advantages and highlight its limitations in current form. Additionally, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of the LGCN's ability to avoid the spirit of the spirit method and plateaus issue in hyperbolic GCNs. To facilitate further research and improve the LGCN, the paper makes the code and datasets publicly available. Future enhancements to the LGCN are also discussed. 

In the context of graph-structured data and manifold learning, GCNs have achieved notable success. This success can be attributed to their ability to leverage local information within graph neighborhoods. However, the process of defining and learning about neighboring patches of a given graph is complicated due to the dynamic nature of the concept 'neighbor'. To address this issue, the paper proposes a theoretical framework for detecting the boundaries of local patch structures based on the curvature of a given manifold. The framework's applicability is demonstrated through the introduction of a new statistic that provides a meaningful way to measure the similarity between neighboring patch embeddings. To incorporate this information into the GCN learning process, a novel convolutional neural network structure called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) is presented. Experimental evaluations conducted on multiple publicly available datasets demonstrate the proposed LGCN's performance advantages over existing hyperbolic GCNs. To facilitate further research and ensure reproducibility of results, the code and datasets used in this study are made available publicly.

This study examines the stability of solutions to the inverse problem of determining a coefficient in the PDE describing a Stefan problem propagation model. This problem involves both heat conduction and surface growth. Using a functional identification method and a modified Stefan iteration technique, we establish a general observability inequality and related Carleman estimate. These results are crucial for achieving optimal stability of solutions in the inverse problem. Furthermore, we prove the existence, uniqueness, and regularity of solutions in this PDE inverse problem. Ultimately, we develop a numerical strategy based on a shape optimization formulation and an iterative algorithm. This approach yields a non-iterative reconstruction method for the free boundary and the unknown coefficient. We validate this method through numerical experiments. As surface growth problems are prone to numerical instability, we also consider a modified approach based on the same observability inequality and observability time, but with a fixed boundary. This modified approach leads to a second numerical strategy and allows us to compare and contrast our results. As such problems often lack a physical basis but offer numerical stability, we refer to them as 'artificial Stefan problems'. Ultimately, we employ these artificial problems to investigate the limitations of the method presented and to assess the impact of noise on our reconstructions. As such, this research contributes to both the inverse problem and the surface growth communities by establishing a link between these two areas and providing a common numerical tool. It is worth noting that the methods introduced in this research are analogous to those employed in the inverse problem community but with respect to the geometry rather than the coefficient, as seen in the research of Beretta, Ito, and Kano, Kim, and Vogelius. Additionally, due to the narrow focus of this research, it is essentially a chapter that has been incorporated into a larger work concerning the determination of free boundaries in a changing medium, which involves both the inverse problem and the determination of front propagation dynamics. It is also essential to acknowledge the contributions of Beretta, Ito, and Kano, Kim, and Vogelius in this regard. It is noteworthy that the method employed in this research can be modified to solve the inverse problem in the case where a coefficient is conserved on the moving front, as this results in a formulation with a constant volume constraint that can be addressed through a similar modification of the shape optimization formulation. The Tsallis distribution has extensive applications in physics, yet its origins remain unclear.  This work proposes a statistical mechanics framework that explains the Tsallis distribution in social systems, using a generalized maximum entropy principle with a weighted average of entropy types. This approach leads to the Tsallis distribution occurring universally, regardless of data specifics.  A study of the Tsallis distribution in the context of its parameters reveals an interesting non-linear relationship, providing an alternative to conventional approaches.  This research offers a theoretical foundation for interpreting the Tsallis distribution and suggests that its characteristics are more important than the specific data generating them.  This is demonstrated empirically using a simple simulation and real-world data, showing that the Tsallis distribution captures system complexity and is more resilient than the normal distribution in the face of data degradation.  This is further illustrated through an example of its practical application in detecting anomalies.  This work is part of a broader study that aims to develop a statistical mechanics framework for understanding social systems and complex phenomena through the lens of non-extensive thermodynamics.  This has already led to the publication of several research findings, including the non- Tsallis cumulant-based coefficient as a earthquake detection indicator in acoustic monitoring, the Tsallis distribution in ground roll noise being beneficial for improving the accuracy of buried object detection, and the non-russian choice of the Tsallis entropy parameter hindering the development of Tsallis-based anomaly detection methods, all of which motivate and are part of this research endeavor.  This work is also related to another research strand that explores the utilization of non-extensive thermodynamics in machine learning, demonstrated through the example of training neural networks with Tsallis-based loss functions and dynamics, showing that they can exhibit complex patterns of their own, providing further understanding of the relationship between entropy, complexity, and the need for regularization in machine learning.  This is illustrated using a generative adversarial network as an example, showing that the Tsallis dynamics prevent the generation of anomalies in the produced data, without compromising its realism. Utilizing a composite vector field model as an illustration, we show that a mass term causes one degree of freedom to become a ghost and another to become a scalar rather than a vector, thereby confirming previous findings by Afshar and Penco. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the inclusion of a mass term breaks screening symmetry, thereby it cannot be a viable dark matter model. A common two-level system analogy involves a spinning top, where its normal positive temperature behavior can be visualized through energy changes as it slows down. However, illustrating negative temperature within this framework proves challenging, as it requires the spinning top to spin at a rate greater than its maximum possible speed, a concept that defies the system's fundamental definition. In contrast, a Markov chain model offers a more straightforward representation of negative temperature, which is directly proportional to the inverse time interval required for the system to return to equilibrium. Furthermore, this model enables the demonstration of negative temperature through the spinning top analogy, in addition to the two-level system analogy. It also facilitates the understanding of negative temperature through the perspective of the spinning top's attempt to escape a stable equilibrium state. In the process, it becomes clear that the term 'negative temperature' is often misinterpreted and confounded with the idea of infinite temperature. It is essential to distinguish these concepts and understand the constraints that must be met for a system to possess negative, zero, or infinite temperatures. In the context of the spinning top, these conditions result in the system having a negative temperature if it is on the verge of collapsing, zero temperature if it is at complete standstill, and infinite temperature if it is spinning at the maximum possible rate. In the case of a Markov chain, these conditions yield a system with negative temperature that is characterized by an asymptotically vanishing inverse time interval, which in turn is marked by a particular sharp spike in the distribution of returned times. Additionally, both the spinning top and the Markov chain models provide insights into the concept of zero temperature, often mistakenly equated with absolute zero, which is actually a state of infinite inverse time interval, implying that zero temperature is actually a state of infinite energy. In the context of the spinning top, this means that zero temperature represents a state of spinning at the maximum possible speed, rather than the absence of motion. It is also demonstrated that the commonly used measure of entropy, the von Neumann entropy, is not a reliable indicator of temperature, as it fails to distinguish between zero and negative temperatures. In contrast, a Negentropy operator is introduced, which is capable of differentiating these temperatures and is thus considered a more suitable measure. A type III seesaw framework is combined with dark parity symmetry to address the dark matter issue and explain the lightweight neutrino mass. The incorporation of a minimal dark sector impacts the vacuum stability and dark parity symmetry within the framework. The condition for dark parity symmetry dictates the range of the dark sector parameter, whereas the interplay between the dark sector mass term and the dark parity symmetry determines the type of vacuum. The minimal setup is analyzed along with the dark parity version of the vacuum stability constraint. The relation between the dark sector mass and the neutrino mass is established. The incorporation of additional dark sector particles can either lower or raise the minimal required inflation scale. The model also meets the requirements for correct big bang nucleosynthesis and the kinetic boundary problem is resolved when the dark sector mass lies within a specific range between $10^{8}$ to $10^{12}$ GeV. The minimal setup matches the predictions of the eta problem for the dark sector scale. The combination of the type III seesaw and the dark parity symmetry leads to the prediction of the active neutrino mass spectrum, specifically the quasi-degenerate case, and the dark matter mass, which can range from $10^{8}$ to $10^{12}$ GeV, depending on the dark parity version of the vacuum. The parameters of the model result in the prediction of the active neutrino mass spectrum, the dark matter mass, and the eta problem scale, which are in agreement with each other. The combination of the type III seesaw and the dark parity symmetry also satisfies the conditions for correct electroweak symmetry breaking and the vacuum stability in the standard model at the renormalization group flow level. The scenario is supported by an analytical expression for the neutrino mass and the dark matter mass in terms of the heavy particle mass in the form of an elliptic curve. The incorporation of additional dark sector particles transforms this curve from an elliptic curve with complex multiplication to a curve of genus one with a CM point. The standard model at the renormalization group flow level is also analyzed along with the prediction of the correct sign for the neutrino mass term and the dark matter mass term. The interplay between the dark sector mass term and the dark parity symmetry also results in the standard model at the renormalization group flow level predicting the correct sign for the theta term in quantum chromodynamics. The consistency of the model is further supported by the absence of the kinetic boundary problem in the standard model at the renormalization group flow level. A critical examination of the effective spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides is undertaken, with a focus on incorporating electron correlation and crystal field splitting. By utilizing a combined strong and weak coupling approach in the framework of multi-orbital lattices, the effective spin-orbit coupling is expressed in terms of interaction effects and crystal field splitting. It is demonstrated that the change in the band filling directly influences the change in the effective spin-orbit coupling, and this phenomenon has been misinterpreted in previous studies. Numerical calculations based on the local density approximation plus Hubbard model are used to validate the theoretical analysis. Furthermore, the application to transition metal oxides is straightforward, with salient features evident in materials such as RuCl$_3$, Sr$_2$IrO$_4$, and Ca$_2$LiNiO$_3$. A comparative analysis of the spin-orbit coupling in head-to-head and tail-to-tail dimer configurations is also presented with a discussion on the magnetic ordering and energy spectrum. Finally, the effective spin-orbit coupling is demonstrated to govern the magnetic ordering in multi-orbital systems. The research focuses on the spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides with the example of Ti-based perovskite, with further examples including BaTiO$_3$, TiO$_2$, and LaTiO$_3$. The results obtained are compared to other studies based on different methodologies. The research has been published in various journals such as Physical Review B, New Journal of Physics, Physical Review Letters, and Physical Review X. The effective spin-orbit coupling has been found to dictate the magnetic ordering in transition metal oxides with correlative tendencies in materials such as Sr$_2$TiO$_4$, TiO$_2$, and LaTiO$_3$. The research on the transition metal oxide Ti-based perovskite also reveals the presence of spin-orbit driven antiferromagnetic ordering in head-to-head dimer configurations. The presence of spin-orbit coupling in Ti-based perovskite is robust, with the effective spin-orbit coupling remaining unaltered across different fillings, with evidence of this robustness in materials such as Sr$_2$TiO$_4$, TiO$_2$, and LaTiO$_3$. Given a normal, complete toric variety, its relative $I$-function can be calculated when a divisor is chosen that meets certain smoothness criteria. For a particular type of variety, known as a toric complete intersection, researchers have discovered that its relative $I$-functions exhibit a interesting pattern of relationship among each other. This guidance can be applied to the broader context of variables and polynomials with specified properties. A notable case study involves Terauds' formula for the relative $I$-functions of a variety with a single divisor. His approach demonstrates how the coefficients of these functions are derived from the edge lengths of a specific join of cones. Additionally, relative $I$-function coefficients for a variety with multiple divisors are found to form an upper triangular matrix. This structure's implications are used to establish the relationship between these coefficients for varieties with diverse geometric configurations. A notable example includes the relative $I$-function coefficients for a specific join of cones, which are displayed in Figure 1. An analysis of these coefficients also leads to the discovery of an identity mirroring the structure of Milnor's duality law. This observation serves as the basis for a proposed conjecture among the paper's main findings. Further, a discussion on the proposed conjecture is presented in the context of a particular example involving a join of cones, as graphically depicted in Figure 2. This example illustrates the step-by-step derivation of relative $I$-function coefficients through the use of local systems. The proposed conjecture is further explored by comparing the results obtained via the local system approach with those generated by the use of Frobenius. A final section is dedicated to outlining the potential directions for future research. These potential areas of study include an examination of the proposed conjecture's generality, as well as an exploration of the relative $I$-function coefficients for varieties with multiple divisors along specific types of curves. Moreover, the paper touches upon the potential connection between the relative $I$-function coefficients and Milnor's duality law within the context of a $d$-dimensional variety with a single divisor. The appendices are utilized to present proofs, discussions, and explanations of various related concepts, including the application of the local system approach to the evaluation of relative $I$-function coefficients for varieties with a single divisor, the analysis of a particular join of cones, an examination of the proposed conjecture's duality aspect, an exploration of the relationship between the relative $I$-function coefficients for varieties

Generative models have the capability to modify input codes to produce different outputs, enabling policy-driven manipulation of generated images. In medical imaging, such techniques hold promise in enhancing clinical decision-making by tailoring the presentation of medical images to specific healthcare professionals' preferences. However, the effectiveness of this approach relies on understanding the underlying representations produced by the model, specifically its latent code. In practice, using latent codes to represent medical conditions in image data might result in representations that are either too general or too specific, thus hindering the policy-driven alteration of images. To address this challenge, we introduce a metric to assess the precision of latent code representations in capturing the distinctions between different medical conditions. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward, policy-free approach to encode medical conditions directly into their corresponding latent codes, facilitating efficient and precise alteration of generated images. Ultimately, our work aims to facilitate the efficient and precise alteration of medical image presentations through efficient policy-free approaches, as demonstrated using a generative adversarial network. The code is available online. When applied to clinical data containing 12 different breast cancer conditions and 1 million natural images, our method successfully distinguishes between 10 different conditions with an accuracy rate of 98.5%, and efficiently alters the presentation of medical images for different healthcare professionals with minimal computational requirements. Furthermore, our results are compatible with various generative models, including models that incorporate external knowledge, and demonstrate a representative performance on multiple medical and natural image datasets. To ensure reproducibility, we have made the code available for the proposed approach and associated metrics on the GTRI Technical Reports website. The efficacy of our approach has significant implications for the policy-driven alteration of medical image presentations, and the code can be utilized by other researchers interested in applying this method to other datasets. The paper also includes several challenging external knowledge representation datasets that can be utilized with our proposed approach, and is accessible online at the GTRI Technical Reports website. The code and datasets can be found at the following link https://ghtr.org/t/2206077201/. ViDaExpert is an interactive visualization software designed to facilitate the exploration of large datasets with numerous dimensions. This tool was developed in response to the limitations of current data visualization expert systems and addresses the challenge of presenting high-dimensional data in a readily interpretable manner. ViDaExpert distinguishes itself through the incorporation of an expert system for visualization that employs a range of techniques such as dimensionality reduction, feature selection, and data transformation to present data in the most effective way possible for both specialists and non-experts. This achievement is made possible by the software's integration of multiple visualization techniques such as 3D surface plotting, hierarchical clustering, and pairwise data comparison. Furthermore, ViDaExpert includes a user-friendly interface that allows users to select the most suitable visualization method for their data and purposes, and also enables them to manipulate visualized data through interactive tools. This assistant is particularly suited for assisting experts in data analysis tasks such as identifying key variables, detecting clusters, and evaluating prediction performance. ViDaExpert's source code is available on GitHub at the time of publication. This software demonstrates the potential benefits of integrating expert systems and visualization technologies for data analysis purposes. Evaluations of ViDaExpert were conducted using real-world datasets related to both machine learning and medical fields, and the results obtained show its effectiveness when compared to other widely-used visualization methods. This project was supported by funds from the Ministry of Science and Technology in Taiwan under the aim of promoting open-source educational tools in computer science. The initial idea for ViDaExpert was conceived based on feedback from students using the previously-mentioned ViDa software, and whose source code is also available on GitHub. This led to ViDaExpert's development as a enhanced and expanded version of ViDa. This project was conducted under the guidance of Yu-Chi Chen and in collaboration with Hsien-Hsu Chen, whose contributions were invaluable. This research was carried out in response to the need for interactive and user-friendly visualization tools in data analysis tasks, and was facilitated by the availability of open-source technologies such as Pygame and scikit-learn. This project also aimed to provide an example of software development that can be used in educational settings, and whose source code can be utilized by students as an example of good coding practice.
